title: Efficacy and safety of filgotinib in patients with active radiographic and nonradiographic axial spondyloarthritis: results from OLINGUITO, a phase 3 trial consisting of 2 randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind, parallel-group studies.
abstract: Objectives This study aimed to investigate the efficacy and safety of filgotinib, a JAK1 preferential inhibitor, in patients with axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA). Methods The phase 3 OLINGUITO trial comprises 2 international, randomised, double-blind, placebo (PBO)-controlled studies. Patients with an established diagnosis of radiographic (r) or nonradiographic (nr) axSpA and an inadequate response/intolerance to ≥2 nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs were randomised 1:1 to filgotinib 200 mg or PBO once daily through week (W) 16 (double-blind period; stratified by high-sensitivity C-reactive protein [hs-CRP] level and prior biologic disease-modifying antirheumatic drug [bDMARD] use). After W16, patients received open-label filgotinib 200 mg through W52; patients ≥65 years and/or with prespecified risk factors received response-based dosing (100 or 200 mg). The primary (Assessment of SpondyloArthritis international Society ≥40% response [ASAS40 response]) and secondary efficacy endpoints were assessed at W16. Efficacy and safety were assessed through W52. Results At W16, the primary endpoint was met in both studies (ASAS40 response rates: r = axSpA [n = 258], 39.5% filgotinib vs 20.9% PBO [P = .001]; nr-axSpA [n = 237], 34.5% vs 17.8% [P = .003], respectively). ASAS40 improvements, irrespective of hs-CRP level/prior bDMARD use, were observed as early as W1. For secondary endpoints, significant improvements were seen in Axial Spondyloarthritis Disease Activity Score and Spondyloarthritis Research Consortium of Canada magnetic resonance imaging sacroiliac joint inflammation in both studies, and in Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Functional Index and Ankylosing Spondylitis Quality of Life Questionnaire in patients with r-axSpA. Improvements with filgotinib were maintained/increased further through W52. Overall, 2 cases of myocardial infarction (PBO: n = 1; PBO-filgotinib: n = 1), 3 of herpes zoster (PBO-filgotinib), and 4 of malignancies (excluding nonmelanoma skin cancer; filgotinib: n = 3; PBO-filgotinib: n = 1) occurred. Conclusions Across the whole spectrum of axSpA, filgotinib provided rapid and significant patient-relevant improvements in axSpA signs and symptoms and was well tolerated.

title: Advanced Image Generation for Cancer and Stem Cell Biology Using Diffusion Models.
abstract: Deep learning has transformed medical image analysis, but progress in cancer and stem cell applications is often constrained by limited access to large, diverse, well-annotated imaging datasets. This bottleneck is especially acute for studies of tumor heterogeneity and cancer stem cell (CSC) biology, where rare phenotypes and dynamic cell-state transitions-frequently linked to stemness-associated transcriptional programs (e.g., OCT4, SOX2, NANOG)-benefit from high-quality imaging across many samples and conditions. At the same time, regulatory and practical barriers (patient privacy, acquisition cost, and uneven institutional data sharing) restrict dataset scale and reuse. Diffusion models offer a practical route to synthetic data expansion by generating high-fidelity synthetic images that retain salient radiologic and pathologic features. In this chapter, we present an end-to-end protocol for adapting latent diffusion (Stable Diffusion) to oncology imaging using DreamBooth fine-tuning with small numbers of representative images, coupled with text-to-image and image-to-image workflows to generate controlled variations across modalities and disease presentations (e.g., brain tumor MRI, breast cancer mammography/CESM). We also describe quantitative and qualitative evaluation strategies, including Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) benchmarking and expert review considerations, to assess realism and diversity. These methods enable cancer and stem cell biologists to augment training data for segmentation and classification, build shareable educational resources, and prototype analyses for rare tumors or stemness-enriched subtypes while potentially reducing reliance on direct sharing of patient images.

title: Thymic Radiation is Associated with Worse Outcomes in Patients with NSCLC.
abstract: Background Emerging evidence indicates the functional importance of the thymus in adult health and may influence oncologic outcomes, yet current radiotherapy (RT) practice does not consider the thymus as an organ of interest. Because RT may incidentally expose the thymus to radiation, we hypothesized that thymic radiation dose is negatively associated with major clinical outcomes. Patients and methods This multicohort analysis included 1,107 patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), including the phase III RTOG-0617 trial (n=460) and two independent real-world cohorts of patients treated with chemoradiotherapy alone (n=422; HARVARD-CRT) or in combination with consolidation immunotherapy (n=225; HARVARD-DURVA). We quantified thymic function using a deep-learning system that assessed thymic radiographic characteristics as a proxy for thymic function. Mean Thymic Dose (MTD) was used to measure thymic radiation exposure. Results Incidental thymic irradiation was associated with increased risk of distant metastases after confounding adjustments. Concretely, a 1Gy increase in MTD was associated with an increased distant metastasis risk of 1.57-4.21% (RTOG-0617: adjusted hazard-ratio [aHR]=1.29; P=0.0028; HARVARD-CRT: aHR=1.33; P=0.011; HARVARD-DURVA: aHR=1.95; P=0.007). In Thymic-Health-stratified analysis, patients with preserved Thymic Health prior to radiotherapy appeared to be at particularly greater risk, whereas no significant associations emerged in patients with impaired Thymic Health. One-year follow-up imaging demonstrated dose-dependent declines in thymic health and lower circulating lymphocyte counts, consistent with a possible biological link between thymic irradiation and immune competence loss. An exploratory feasibility study suggested that re-optimizing RT planning for thymic sparing can be achieved without compromising tumor coverage or cardiopulmonary constraints. Conclusions Thymic radiation exposure was independently associated with higher risks of metastasis and death in NSCLC patients, especially in those with preserved thymic function. These findings raise awareness towards considering the thymus as an organ of interest in radiotherapy and suggest that thymus-sparing strategies may help preserve immune health and improve patient outcomes.

title: [THE ROLE OF AI TECHNOLOGY IN MAMMOGRAPHIC SCREENING OF BREAST CANCER WITH EVALUATION OF EFFICIENCY AND POTENTIAL FOR PRACTICAL HEALTH CARE].
abstract: In conditions of increasing workload on organized mammographic screening programs and deficiency of qualified personnel, implementation of auxiliary technologies on the basis of artificial intelligence (AI) acquires special actuality. The results of retrospective cohort study included 100 histologically verified cases of breast cancer (BI-RADS category 6) permitted to evaluate diagnostic efficiency of AI algorithm as compared to independent conclusions of three certified radiologists with length of service more than 10 years. The sensitivity of technology of AI amounted 86%-96%, depending on dichotomization model. The percentage of total coincidence with appraisal of experts varied within the limits 87-91%. The level of concordance, assessed using weighted Cohen's kappa coefficient, came up to κq = 0.76 (95% CI: 0.68-0.83) that corresponds to "good" concordance. In 1%-3% of cases, the AI algorithm identified suspicious findings missed by experts, at that without increasing volume of groundless examinations due to conservative classification of most disputable cases as BI-RADS 3 with ordering dynamic observation. The obtained results confirm clinical applicability of AI technology as standardizing and relieving tool in practical health care, capable to increase sensitivity of screening and to decrease risk of false-negative conclusions without violation of established clinical protocols.

title: Side-Step Cutting Foot Biomechanics and Intrinsic Foot Muscle Sizes in People With Chronic Ankle Instability.
abstract: Introduction Lateral ankle sprains commonly occur during directional changes and often lead to chronic ankle instability (CAI) associated with altered movement patterns, muscle weakness and atrophy. This study aimed to compare foot joint biomechanics during cutting among individuals with CAI, copers, and uninjured controls and to explore the relationship between intrinsic foot muscle sizes and functional status. Methods Cross-sectional study. Sixty-nine recreationally active males (25.4 ± 4 years) were categorised by perceived instability and self-reported function. Ankle and foot joint kinematics and kinetics were assessed using a multi-segment foot model during 45° side-step cutting at a mean approach speed of 3.5 m·s -1 . Groups were compared using ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis tests, and continuous biomechanical data were analysed using statistical parametric or non-parametric mapping. Cross-sectional area and thickness of the abductor hallucis and flexor digitorum brevis were recorded using ultrasound imaging. Muscle sizes were explored using general linear models, and correlations with questionnaire scores and physical examination outcomes were calculated. Results Foot joint kinematics and kinetics did not significantly differ between the groups. Individuals with CAI exhibited lower peak posterior ground reaction force than controls (mean difference: -6.2% of body weight, 95% CI: -11.9 to -0.4, p = 0.03). Statistical parametric mapping revealed lower posterior ground reaction forces from 22% to 46% of stance in CAI versus controls (p < 0.05). Intrinsic foot muscle sizes showed weak, statistically significant negative correlations with perceived instability scores (ρ = -0.31 to -0.36) and self-reported function scores (ρ = -0.26 to -0.33). Conclusion Despite pronounced sensory-perceptual impairments, individuals with CAI demonstrated few differences in foot joint biomechanics compared with copers and controls during a moderate-speed anticipated cutting task. Reduced braking forces may reflect altered deceleration strategies. These findings suggest the importance of assessing deceleration abilities in people with CAI and indicate a potential role of foot muscles in CAI-related functional outcomes. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05815576).

Groups were compared using ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis tests, and continuous biomechanical data were analysed using statistical parametric or non-parametric mapping. Cross-sectional area and thickness of the abductor hallucis and flexor digitorum brevis were recorded using ultrasound imaging. Muscle sizes were explored using general linear models, and correlations with questionnaire scores and physical examination outcomes were calculated.

Results

Foot joint kinematics and kinetics did not significantly differ between the groups. Individuals with CAI exhibited lower peak posterior ground reaction force than controls (mean difference: -6.2% of body weight, 95% CI: -11.9 to -0.4, p = 0.03). Statistical parametric mapping revealed lower posterior ground reaction forces from 22% to 46% of stance in CAI versus controls (p < 0.05). Intrinsic foot muscle sizes showed weak, statistically significant negative correlations with perceived instability scores (ρ = -0.31 to -0.36) and self-reported function scores (ρ = -0.26 to -0.33).

Conclusion

Despite pronounced sensory-perceptual impairments, individuals with CAI demonstrated few differences in foot joint biomechanics compared with copers and controls during a moderate-speed anticipated cutting task. Reduced braking forces may reflect altered deceleration strategies. These findings suggest the importance of assessing deceleration abilities in people with CAI and indicate a potential role of foot muscles in CAI-related functional outcomes.

title: Concordance of Microbiological and Histopathological Examination of Bone Biopsies in Diagnosing Diabetic Foot Osteomyelitis, a Systematic Review.
abstract: Background Diabetic foot osteomyelitis (DFO) is a serious complication of diabetic foot ulcers and is associated with increased risk of amputation, morbidity, and mortality. Bone biopsy remains the most definitive diagnostic modality, yet controversy persists over its diagnostic utility This study reviews the diagnostic concordance of histopathology and microbiology in bone biopsy specimens from patients with DFO and examines the clinical implications of the findings. Methods A systematic review was conducted using PubMed, Medline, CINHAL, Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar. Studies included adult patients with DFO in whom bone biopsy specimens underwent both histopathological and microbiological analysis. Five core studies met the eligibility criteria. Data on study design, setting, population, diagnostic methods, concordance rates, and outcomes were extracted and synthesized utilising a quantitative narrative synthesis. Results Across the five studies (n = 308 patients), histopathology and microbiology showed modest concordance, with mean rates of concordant positive results of 43.4% and common discordant findings. Histopathology demonstrated higher specificity, while microbiology had higher sensitivity, ranging from 70% to 83.9% but greater susceptibility to contamination. Positive histopathology was more strongly associated with the need for revision surgery or extended antibiotic therapy. Discussion Histopathology appears to offer superior diagnostic specificity, whereas microbiology provides valuable information for antimicrobial management. Frequent discordance underscores the importance of interpreting results in a clinical context. Further robust, prospective studies are needed to clarify the optimal diagnostic approach and standardise definitions.

title: Prevalence of Hallux Valgus in Patients With Femoral Neck Fracture and Its Association With Postoperative Functional Outcomes.
abstract: Background Hallux valgus is a frequent forefoot deformity in older adults and has been linked to impaired balance, gait dysfunction, and increased fall risk. However, its prevalence among patients with femoral neck fracture and its association with postoperative functional outcomes remain unclear. Methods This single-center retrospective study included 235 patients aged ≥ 65 years with available radiographic data who underwent surgery for femoral neck fracture between 2022 and 2024. Hallux valgus was defined on weight-bearing radiographs as a hallux valgus angle (HVA) ≥ 20°. Functional outcomes were evaluated using the Functional Independence Measure (FIM) at 3 months postoperatively. Multivariable linear regression analysis was performed to determine whether hallux valgus was independently associated with motor FIM scores after adjustment for age, sex, surgical procedure, and cognitive function. Results Among the 235 patients with radiographic data, 178 (76%) were women, with a median age of 85 (77-90) years; 86% of patients underwent bipolar hemiarthroplasty. Hallux valgus was present in 55% (130/235), including 20% (47/235) with moderate-to-severe deformity (HVA ≥ 30°). Patients with hallux valgus had significantly lower motor FIM scores at 3 months than those without the deformity (p = 0.044), whereas cognitive and total FIM scores did not differ. In multivariable analysis, hallux valgus (HVA ≥ 20°) was independently associated with lower motor FIM scores (B = -5.92, 95% CI -10.95 to -0.89; p = 0.021). Conclusions Hallux valgus is highly prevalent in patients with femoral neck fracture and is independently associated with lower postoperative motor function. Assessment of hallux valgus may provide additional insight into postoperative functional prognosis in this population.

title: Clinical Correlations Between Diagnostic Assessment Methods and Functional Outcomes in Musculoskeletal Rehabilitation: A Narrative Review.
abstract: Background Musculoskeletal disorders are major contributors to pain, disability, reduced participation, and health-care utilisation. Structural and digital diagnostic tools can characterise pathology, but their ability to explain functional limitations and rehabilitation prognosis is often incomplete. This narrative review aimed to synthesise representative evidence on the relationship between diagnostic and screening methods and functional outcomes in musculoskeletal rehabilitation, with emphasis on clinical interpretation and practical use in care pathways. Methods Peer-reviewed literature, supplemented by manual screening of relevant reference lists, was reviewed to identify publications available through March 2026. The synthesis prioritised studies linking diagnostic findings to patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs), performance-based tests, or real-world activity metrics. Results Conventional imaging, including ultrasound, computed tomography, and MRI, may identify clinically relevant pathology but often shows only modest concordance with pain, disability, and performance-based function. PROMs and brief performance tests provide the most direct functional anchors, whereas interpretation using the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) or responder thresholds is needed to distinguish statistically detectable associations from clinically meaningful change. Biomarkers and AI-supported analytics remain promising but insufficiently validated for independent functional prognostication. Wearable sensors appear most clinically useful for longitudinal monitoring of real-world activity, and brief psychosocial screening helps explain the discordance between structural findings and perceived disability. Conclusion Functional prognosis in musculoskeletal rehabilitation should not rely on diagnostic findings alone. A multidimensional, function-centred first-visit bundle combining focused examination, one region-specific PROM, one brief performance test, and brief psychosocial risk screening may improve triage, patient communication, rehabilitation planning, and follow-up. Diagnostic escalation should be selective and reserved for red flags, management-changing pathology, or failure to improve on repeated standardised functional reassessment.

title: Whole-Brain 4D MRA With Improved Vessel Delineation Using Undersampled Multiple Overlapping Thin-Slab Radial Acquisition.
abstract: Time-resolved arterial spin labeling (ASL)-based noncontrast 4D MRA enables visualization of cerebral arterial flow dynamic patterns and holds great potential for evaluating cerebrovascular disease. However, conventional ASL 4D MRA implementations using look-locker acquisitions are susceptible to progressive RF saturation during extended readouts, leading to substantial ASL signal attenuation and loss of vessel delineation in distal arteries. These limitations potentially hinder a wider clinical translation of 4D MRA, especially when assessment of whole-brain vascular anatomy and flow dynamics is needed. This study introduces a practical and reliable ASL 4D MRA technique for whole-brain or large volumetric imaging by integrating pulsed ASL with undersampled multiple overlapping thin-slab stack-of-stars (SOS) golden-angle radial acquisition. The proposed method was evaluated against conventional single-slab 4D MRA, 3D time-of-flight magnetic resonance angiography (TOF-MRA), and pseudocontinuous ASL (pCASL)-based 4D MRA in terms of vessel delineation, blood flow dynamics, and image quality. Compared to the other methods, the proposed method substantially reduced RF saturation effects and preserved signal intensities in distal small arteries, resulting in significantly improved vessel continuity and contrast throughout the cerebral vasculature, as well as reliably capturing complete inflow-to-outflow arterial flow dynamics with good scan efficiency and image quality. The proposed technique enables high-quality, time-resolved whole-brain angiography, offering a promising noncontrast imaging tool for comprehensive assessment of cerebral arterial hemodynamics in clinical and research applications.

title: Quantitative Chemical Exchange Saturation Transfer Imaging With Golden-Angle Radial k-Space Sampling and Locally Low-Rank Reconstruction.
abstract: Chemical exchange saturation transfer magnetic resonance fingerprinting (CEST-MRF) is a promising quantitative molecular imaging technique. To reduce scan time, current CEST-MRF implementations typically use echo-planar imaging (EPI) readouts, which are prone to geometric distortion and signal dropout. In this study, we developed a motion-robust, geometrically accurate CEST-MRF method using radial k-space sampling, locally low-rank reconstruction, and neural network-based quantification. The acquisition schedule was optimized using deep learning, and its accuracy was validated in numerical simulations with digital phantoms. The number of spokes per measurement was determined through simulations and in vivo ablation studies in healthy volunteers. Five healthy subjects underwent repeated scans, and regions of interest were defined for analysis. Tissue maps generated with the proposed method were compared with values obtained from nonlinear least-squares (NLS) fitting of multisaturation-power z-spectra. Motion sensitivity and test-retest reproducibility were evaluated using the coefficient of variation (CV) and intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). Clinical feasibility was demonstrated in a subject with a history of remote middle cerebral artery infarction. The results show that 3D quantitative CEST maps can be acquired in 11 min using 34 spokes per measurement. Numerical simulations yielded mean errors below 14% for all tissue parameters, while in vivo parameter estimates agreed well with both NLS-derived values and prior brain CEST-MRF studies. The mean ICC across all tissue maps was 0.92 in white matter and 0.87 in gray matter, with mean intersubject CVs of 5.4% and 3.4%, respectively. The mean error between motion and no-motion conditions was 8.6%. In the pathology case, changes in CEST-MRF tissue parameters were consistent with clinically diagnosed cystic gliosis. This approach enables accurate and reproducible 3D quantitative CEST imaging of the brain within clinically feasible scan times.

title: Therapeutic efficacy of naloxone hydrochloride combined with hemoperfusion in toxic acute renal failure via the oxidative stress/Nrf2 pathway .
abstract: Background Toxic acute renal failure (ARF) involves severe oxidative stress. The Nrf2 pathway is a key antioxidant defense mechanism. Objectives To investigate whether naloxone combined with hemoperfusion alleviates oxidative injury via Nrf2 activation in toxic ARF. Methods In this single-center retrospective cohort study at Qiqihar Medical University Hospital, 67 patients were enrolled through medical record screening. The control group (n=39) received hemoperfusion alone; the observation group (n=28) received additional intravenous naloxone (0.8 mg bolus + 2.0 mg/24 h infusion for 7 days). Renal function and oxidative markers were assessed before treatment, at 24 h and day 7. Multivariate regression analysis was used to adjust for confounding factors. Separately, 30 rats were randomized into control, model and treatment groups (n=10 each). The treatment group received intraperitoneal naloxone (1.0 mg/kg) plus simulated hemoperfusion. Results After adjusting for baseline imbalances, combined therapy was independently associated with significant reductions in Scr and BUN in patients (adjusted β = -8.52, 95% CI: -12.37 to -4.67, P < 0.001) and with significant improvements in renal function and histopathology in rats. Combined therapy decreased tubular injury markers (β2-MG, KIM-1, NGAL, L-FABP) in rats. Mechanistically, it was associated with activation of the Nrf2/HO-1/NQO1 pathway, enhanced SOD activity and reduced MDA levels. Improvements were time-dependent (24 h to day 7). Conclusions Naloxone combined with hemoperfusion activates the Nrf2 pathway, attenuates oxidative stress and improves renal function in toxic acute renal failure.

title: The Ataxias as an Example of Rare Diseases: Diagnosis, Genetics, and Treatment.
abstract: Background Ataxias are a group of rare diseases. In the European Union, a disease is defined as rare if its prevalence is less than 5 per 10 000 people. Ataxias are rarer than this threshold, although reliable prevalence estimates are largely lacking. The worldwide mean prevalence of autosomal dominant hereditary ataxias is approximately 2.7 per 100 000 people (95% confidence interval [1.5; 4.0/100 000]), and that of autosomal-recessive ataxias is approximately 3.3 per 100 000 people [1.8; 4.9/100 000]. Ataxias include hereditary (genetic), sporadic degenerative, and acquired types. Methods This narrative review is based on the guidelines of the German Society for Neurology ( Deutsche Gesellschaft für Neurologie ) and on other current reviews, supplemented by the findings of targeted PubMed searches. Results In the more common types of hereditary ataxia, a presumptive diagnosis (spot diagnosis) can already be made on the basis of the history, neurological examination, and brain MRI findings and can then be confirmed by genetic testing. These include Friedreich ataxia, the RFC1-CANVAS syndrome (cerebellar ataxia, neuropathy, and vestibular areflexia), and spinocerebellar ataxia types 3 and 27B (SCA3 and SCA27B). When a spot diagnosis is not possible, the diagnosis can often be established by genetic testing (preferably genome-based). Multisystem atrophy of the cerebellar type (MSA-C) arises sporadically. Opportunities for treatment remain limited, but many new therapies are under development, including gene therapy.

title: An X-ray micro-CT protocol enables non-destructive 3D visualization of glandular architecture in archived paraffin-embedded prostate cancer tissue.
abstract: The prostate is organized as a complex glandular network, and prostate cancer is accompanied by architectural changes that cannot always be inferred from two-dimensional (2D) histology. The study of these features in three dimensions (3D) in cancerous tissue is important because glandular features have shown potential value for disease characterization and risk stratification beyond that obtained from individual 2D sections. Large collections of clinically annotated material preserved in paraffin remain an important research source. However, many 3D imaging methods require destructive or labor-intensive preparation, limiting access to valuable material that needs to be re-archived. In this proof-of-concept study, we developed an X-ray micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) workflow for direct 3D imaging of archived paraffin-embedded prostate specimens with near-zero sample manipulation. Imaging and denoising parameters were optimized to balance image quality with acquisition time. Paraffin-embedded prostate core punches (n = 5) from five radical prostatectomy specimens were imaged by micro-CT and subsequently processed for histology. Digitized histological sections were aligned with corresponding micro-CT planes for qualitative comparison, while pre-sectioning micro-CT data provided an intact geometric reference for exploratory assessment of histology-associated dimensional changes at the whole-core and glandular-lumen levels. The optimized workflow yielded micro-CT images with discernible glandular morphology and qualitative structural correspondence with matched histological sections. Exploratory measurements suggested modest dimensional change at the whole-core level and greater variability at the lumen level; none of the tested deformation metrics reached conventional statistical significance. Illustrative 3D segmentation presented the glandular epithelium and lumina as spatially continuous structures within a cancer-containing region. These findings support the feasibility of X-ray micro-CT as a non-destructive approach for 3D characterization of prostate glandular architecture directly from paraffin-embedded tissue, providing volumetric context for structures identified on histology while preserving the specimen for subsequent histological assessment.

title: Diagnostic image quality of shoulder magnetic resonance imaging at 0.55T in healthy subjects and patients with rotator cuff injury: Prospective comparison with 1.5T.
abstract: Background Lower‑field 0.55 T MRI scanners with large‑bore design could offer patients more comfortable feeling and flexible position. With the advances in deep‑learning reconstruction and hardware optimization, 0.55T have greatly improved their image quality and cost‑effectiveness for musculoskeletal applications. However, its feasibility for shoulder evaluation remains unstudied. Purpose To evaluate the image quality of shoulder using 0.55T MRI in volunteers and patients with rotator cuff injury with comparison of conventional 1.5T. Methods Fifty participants (25 volunteers, 25 patients) were prospectively enrolled. All participants underwent shoulder MRI both at open 0.55T with contour coils and deep learning (DL) and 1.5T MR without DL. The nonparametric method was utilized to compare image quality scores and quantitative metrics (signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and contrast-to-noise ratio (|CNR|)). Arthroscopy have been conducted in 16 patients. Kappa statistics was used to assess interobserver and interstudy agreement for lesion evaluation. Comfort feeling was also compared. Results The scan time was 11'25″ for 0.55T MRI and 11'42″ for 1.5T MRI. The interobserver analyses showed high consistency (κ = 0.771-1.000, P: 0.008 ∼ < 0.001) among 3 readers. The scores for coronal fat suppressed T2 weighted imaging (fsT2WI) and coronal T1 weighted imaging (T1WI) were significantly higher for 0.55T MRI. Most sequences at 0.55T demonstrated significantly higher SNRs (P:0.04 ∼ < 0.001). Additionally, |CNR| values for lesions were significantly higher in fs proton weighted imaging (PDWI) and fsT2WI at 0.55T. Perfect interstudy agreement between 0.55T and 1.5T was observed between 2 readers (Kappa = 1, P < 0.001) for lesion assessment. Agreement between MRI findings and arthroscopic results was perfect or good. The 0.55T system received higher scores in comfort ratings. Conclusion The 0.55T MRI with DL, showed comparable or better image quality in healthy subjects and patients with rotator cuff injury to 1.5T MRI without DL.

title: Synthetic MRI from radiotherapy planning CT images for Head-and-Neck Cancer.
abstract: Background Computed Tomography (CT) provides geometric accuracy and electron density information essential for radiotherapy planning; however, it offers limited soft-tissue contrast. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) improves tumor visualization but introduces registration uncertainties when acquired separately from the radiotherapy planning CT (pCT). Cross-modality image synthesis enables the generation of synthetic MRI (sMRI) directly from pCT and may combine the strengths of both modalities, reducing reliance on MRI access. Purpose We propose a two-stage deep-learning framework for generating sMRI from pCT image-sets specifically in head-and-neck (H&N) cancers, providing soft-tissue contrast comparable to ground-truth MR images (gtMRI). Methods This study included 60 patient cases with H&N cancer treated with radical radiotherapy between March 2022 and April 2024 for model development (50 for training, 10 for validation), plus 10 additional cases, independent of the development cohort for testing. All patients underwent a standard, non-contrast pCT scan followed by an MRI acquired on a 3T Siemens MR simulator. Images were deformably-registered, yielding 10,000 matched CT-MRI slice-pairs for model training. The proposed model utilizes a two-stage architecture, a Pix2Pix conditional generative adversarial network (GAN) for coarse sMRI synthesis, followed by a conditional diffusion model for refinement. To test the model's robustness, 10 patient cases with both pCT and contrast-enhanced CT (ceCT) were used to generate sMRI. Model performance was assessed using structural similarity index (SSIM), multi-scale structural similarity index (MS-SSIM), mean absolute error (MAE), and peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR). In addition, the geometric agreement of the primary (GTVp_70) and nodal (GTVn_70) gross tumor volumes delineated on sMRI vs. gtMRI was independently assessed by two radiation oncologists (ROs) using the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), 95 th -percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95), and average symmetric surface distance (ASSD). Results The average MS-SSIM, SSIM, MAE and PSNR for pCT-derived sMRI were 0.82 ± 0.02, 0.70 ± 0.03, 0.05 ± 0.01, and 20.42 ± 0.66 dB, respectively. The mean MS-SSIM and SSIM values for ceCT-derived sMRI were 0.02 lower than those for the corresponding pCT-to-sMRI metrics. For the contour-based evaluation, sMRI-derived GTV contours achieved a mean DSC of 0.56 and 0.60 for GTVp_70, and 0.72 and 0.74 for GTVn_70 across the two ROs, relative to gtMRI contours. Conclusion Our proof-of-concept study demonstrates the feasibility of pCT-derived sMRI for H&N cancers using a deep-learning framework. The model produces grayscale patterns and soft-tissue contrast that closely resemble the gtMRI.

title: Image quality robustness of HyperSight-enabled versus conventional iterative cone-beam CT across patient size and imaging geometry.
abstract: Background Recent advances in cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) have led to the development of next-generation CBCT systems with enhanced image quality and quantitative imaging capabilities. These advances are particularly relevant in the context adaptive radiation therapy, where improved soft tissue visualization and Hounsfield unit (HU) stability are increasingly important for target localization and CBCT-based dose calculation. Purpose To determine how image quality and HU stability change with increasing phantom size, non-cylindrical geometries, and exposure level, and compare the robustness of Acuros-based HyperSight-enabled iterative CBCT (HS-iCBCT) and conventional iterative CBCT on a TrueBeam (TB-iCBCT) under these conditions. Methods The CatPhan® 604 phantom, combined with custom annular extensions, was used to simulate increasing patient size and non-cylindrical imaging geometries. Three configurations (no annulus, small annulus, and large annulus) were imaged across a range of exposure levels (mAs) using HS-iCBCT and TB-iCBCT. Image evaluation metrics included noise, contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), low-contrast visibility (LCV), image uniformity, spatial resolution, and Hounsfield unit (HU) constancy. Results For the no-annulus configuration, image quality was comparable between systems, with slightly lower noise observed for TB-iCBCT. With increasing phantom size through the added annuli, TB-iCBCT exhibited substantial degradation in noise, contrast, and uniformity, whereas HS-iCBCT maintained more consistent performance. Spatial resolution was primarily dependent on field of view and was similar between systems, with smaller fields of view provided improved spatial resolution. HU constancy degraded with increasing phantom size and material density for both systems but remained substantially more stable for HS-iCBCT. Conclusions HS-iCBCT demonstrated improved robustness to patient size and imaging geometry, providing superior image quality and HU stability compared to TB-iCBCT. These improvements may support potential lower-dose imaging and more reliable performance in larger patients and non-cylindrical imaging geometries commonly encountered in clinical radiotherapy.

title: Generative artificial intelligence in medical oncology: A clinically focused narrative review of large language, vision-language, and agentic artificial intelligence systems.
abstract: Rapid advances in cancer genetics and genomics, pathophysiology, diagnostics, and therapeutics have substantially increased the complexity of clinical oncology. Integrating large and diverse data streams into timely, patient-specific decisions provides a compelling rationale for incorporating artificial intelligence (AI) into cancer care. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) encompasses several classes of models capable of generating new content. This clinically focused review concentrates on GenAI applications based primarily on large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs), as well as emerging agentic systems that use these models to perform coordinated, multistep tasks. LLMs demonstrate substantial medical knowledge, strong performance on oncology-related assessments, and emerging capabilities in clinical reasoning. Guideline- and retrieval-augmented systems can improve concordance with expert recommendations and interpretation of complex treatment algorithms. LLMs and VLMs have been applied to documentation, patient communication, information extraction and summarization, clinical decision support, and multimodal data synthesis. However, performance varies substantially across tasks and clinical domains, with important limitations including incomplete or outdated information, training-data bias, automation bias, and confabulation. Agentic AI represents an emerging extension of these technologies in which LLMs or VLMs are incorporated into systems capable of multistep planning, external information retrieval, specialized tool use, and iterative evaluation and refinement. Early oncology applications include evidence synthesis, multimodal clinical decision support, radiology, pathology, surgery, and individualized treatment planning. With rigorous validation, transparent implementation, continual updating, and appropriate expert oversight, GenAI may augment oncologists' judgment, improve patient understanding and experience, streamline cancer care delivery, and advance personalized oncology.

title: Non-small cell lung carcinoma and its mimics on cytology and small biopsy samples: a practical approach aligned with the WHO Reporting System.
abstract: Accurate classification of lung tumors in cytology specimens and small biopsies remains a diagnostic challenge because of limited cellularity, preanalytical variables, and significant morphologic overlap among entities. This review summarizes key cytomorphologic characteristics and practical immunocytochemical strategies, and common diagnostic pitfalls encountered in the evaluation of non-small cell lung carcinoma, small cell lung carcinoma, neuroendocrine tumors, secondary pulmonary neoplasms, and uncommon thoracic entities in endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration and fine-needle aspiration samples. Particular emphasis is placed on the appropriate use of limited immunohistochemical panels to optimize tumor subtyping while preserving material for molecular testing. Diagnostic challenges such as crush artifact, necrosis, reactive mimics, overlapping morphologic patterns, and the risk of misclassification of rare tumors are addressed with practical guidance for differential diagnosis. By integrating morphologic assessment with ancillary testing, cytopathologists can achieve accurate tumor subtyping, distinguish mimics, and provide precise diagnoses that guide clinical management and selection of targeted therapies.

title: Structural Reorganization of Hypothalamic Subfields in Postherpetic Neuralgia: Volumetric and Morphometric Covariance Network Analyses.
abstract: Background Postherpetic neuralgia (PHN) is a chronic neuropathic pain condition associated with central nervous system reorganization, but hypothalamic alterations remain poorly understood. We investigated hypothalamic subfield volumes and morphometric covariance network organization in patients with PHN. Methods This prospective cross-sectional study included 42 patients with PHN and 41 healthy controls whose hypothalamic subfield volumes were obtained from T1-weighted MRI using automated FreeSurfer segmentation. Bilateral mean raw subfield volumes were compared between groups using analysis of covariance, adjusting for age, sex and estimated total intracranial volume, with false discovery rate correction for multiple comparisons. Morphometric covariance networks were constructed from age- and sex-residualized subfield volumes and graph-theoretical measures were compared using permutation testing. Results After adjustment for estimated total intracranial volume, age and sex, the tubular superior subfield was nominally larger in PHN (adjusted difference, 4.95 mm 3 ; 95% CI, 0.05-9.85; p = 0.048), but did not survive FDR correction. No other subfield or whole-hypothalamic volume differed significantly. PHN showed reduced local efficiency and clustering coefficient and increased characteristic path length, without a significant difference in global efficiency. No pain-side-dependent lateralization or significant associations between subfield volumes and pain measures or disease duration were observed. Conclusions PHN was associated with altered hypothalamic morphometric covariance organization, characterized by reduced local network segregation and increased characteristic path length, while regional volume differences were limited after intracranial volume correction. These findings suggest that PHN-related central reorganization may involve hypothalamic systems related to homeostatic regulation and stress adaptation. Significance statement This study demonstrates altered morphometric covariance organization of hypothalamic subfields in postherpetic neuralgia, despite limited evidence of regional volumetric differences after intracranial volume adjustment. These findings suggest that hypothalamic involvement in PHN may be better reflected by altered coordinated structural organization than by regional volume changes alone.

Methods

This prospective cross-sectional study included 42 patients with PHN and 41 healthy controls whose hypothalamic subfield volumes were obtained from T1-weighted MRI using automated FreeSurfer segmentation. Bilateral mean raw subfield volumes were compared between groups using analysis of covariance, adjusting for age, sex and estimated total intracranial volume, with false discovery rate correction for multiple comparisons. Morphometric covariance networks were constructed from age- and sex-residualized subfield volumes and graph-theoretical measures were compared using permutation testing.

Results

After adjustment for estimated total intracranial volume, age and sex, the tubular superior subfield was nominally larger in PHN (adjusted difference, 4.95 mm3; 95% CI, 0.05-9.85; p = 0.048), but did not survive FDR correction. No other subfield or whole-hypothalamic volume differed significantly. PHN showed reduced local efficiency and clustering coefficient and increased characteristic path length, without a significant difference in global efficiency. No pain-side-dependent lateralization or significant associations between subfield volumes and pain measures or disease duration were observed.

Conclusions

PHN was associated with altered hypothalamic morphometric covariance organization, characterized by reduced local network segregation and increased characteristic path length, while regional volume differences were limited after intracranial volume correction. These findings suggest that PHN-related central reorganization may involve hypothalamic systems related to homeostatic regulation and stress adaptation.

Significance statement

This study demonstrates altered morphometric covariance organization of hypothalamic subfields in postherpetic neuralgia, despite limited evidence of regional volumetric differences after intracranial volume adjustment. These findings suggest that hypothalamic involvement in PHN may be better reflected by altered coordinated structural organization than by regional volume changes alone.

title: Combined PET imaging of tumor hypoxia and proliferation in Glioblastoma using a single injection of 18F-FMISO and 18F-FLT: Association with sites of subsequent recurrence.
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is characterized by intra-tumoral heterogeneity, rapid proliferation, hypoxia-driven radio-resistance, and early recurrence. Gadolinium-Enhanced MRI, the standard of care imaging modality for surgical and radiotherapy planning, lacks specificity for viable tumor burden, particularly in non-enhancing regions. This pilot study aimed to evaluate whether preoperative dual-tracer PET using a combined dose of 18FMISO (hypoxia) and 18FLT (proliferation) improves tumor delineation and predicts subsequent local recurrence compared with MRI. Seven patients with WHO grade 4 gliomas (5 GBM, 2 IDH-mutant astrocytomas) underwent preoperative dual-[FMISO+FLT] static PET at 180 min post-injection, and MRI. 6/7 patients underwent resection. Tumor volumes were segmented from PET, contrast-enhanced T1 (T1-Gd), and T2-FLAIR. Postoperative resection cavities were delineated, and follow-up MRI every 3 months was used to identify recurrence. PET-defined tumor volumes extending beyond resection were correlated with subsequent recurrence sites. Thirteen lesions were analyzed; all showed [FMISO+FLT] uptake (mean activity concentration ratio 1.6 with the cerebellar cortex used as reference region). PET-defined tumor volumes (9.2 cc) were slightly larger than T1-Gd (7.9 cc) but smaller than T2-FLAIR (28.8 cc). PET-defined volumes frequently extended beyond MRI-defined contours (mean non-overlap 6.4 cc vs T1-Gd; 1.5 cc vs. T2-FLAIR). Of six patients undergoing resection, four developed local recurrence within 3.3 months. In all cases, recurrence arose within PET-avid regions outside the resection cavity. The other two patients with complete resection of PET-defined volumes showed a relatively prolonged progression-free-survival (PFS) and including one patient with overall survival exceeding 36 months. Dual-[FMISO+FLT] PET is feasible, safe, and can allow delineation of biologically viable tumor subregions, in particular within the MRI T2-FLAIR volume. This approach prospectively identified sites of subsequent local recurrence and may improve surgical planning and radiotherapy dose escalation. Larger validation studies are warranted to establish dual-tracer PET as a precision imaging paradigm in GBM.

title: Learning global and local representations for generalized category discovery in neurodegenerative diseases.
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has achieved notable success in closed-set classification of neurodegenerative diseases, but its performance degrades significantly in more realistic open-set settings, such as discovering rare or novel disease subtypes from unlabeled data that are not seen during training. This study introduces, to our knowledge, the first framework for generalized category discovery (GCD) in neurodegenerative diseases using MRI. It aims to leverage labeled data from known categories to automatically identify novel categories within unlabeled datasets. We propose a GCD framework integrating semi-supervised contrastive learning with global-local representation learning to jointly optimize feature learning. Globally, we enforce consistency between weakly augmented views of the same instance by aligning their similarity relationships with other embeddings in a support queue. Locally, we treat neighborhood embeddings from the support queue as positive pairs for cross-instance contrastive learning, enhancing fine-grained discrimination. This dual strategy results in a unified learning objective that is applicable to both labeled and unlabeled data, effectively narrowing the representation gap among semantically similar instances. We evaluate our method on a benchmark dataset comprising six neurodegenerative diseases, with over 1500 patient samples. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework consistently outperforms representative state-of-the-art methods. Specifically, our method achieves 66.02% Accuracy and 60.59% Normalized Mutual Information on all categories, and 54.53% Accuracy and 16.67% Normalized Mutual Information on novel categories, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods. Our framework underscores the model's robustness and its practical value in discovering new neurodegenerative disease conditions, highlighting its potential for advancing open-set diagnostic AI.

title: Artificial intelligence apps for medical image analysis using pyCERR and cancer genomics cloud.
abstract: Purpose To provide a software resource that enables medical researchers and practitioners to develop and apply reproducible, out-of-the-box, AI-based analysis workflows for radiological and radiotherapy data. Development and validation methods The framework comprises two main components: the Python-native computational environment for radiological research (pyCERR) for radiological image processing, and the cancer genomics cloud (CGC), a National Cancer Institute-funded resource that supports cloud-hosted collaborative projects, with tools for managing collaborators and compute-hardware from providers such as Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud Platform. pyCERR is open-source (GNU GPL) and distributed at https://github.com/cerr/pycerr; it provides user-friendly data structures, simplified access to metadata across radiological imaging modalities, and tools for data transformation, AI-based image segmentation, radiomics, dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI analysis, radiotherapy dose-volume histogram (DVH) feature extraction, and normal-tissue complication and tumor-control models. Radiomics features comply with the Image biomarker standardization initiative (IBSI) standards and are validated against published reference values. Unit tests covering data input/output, radiomics, DVH features, and visualization run on every code update. Workflows are containerized for reproducible, identical execution on the CGC and on local hardware. The CGC enables AI inference from radiological images to be combined with other data types such as genomics and proteomics. Our public CGC project (https://cgc.sbgenomics.com/u/sevenbridges/pycerr-radiological-radiotherapy-imageanalysis), accessible with free registration, currently includes apps for organ-at-risk (OAR) and lung-nodule segmentation based on published models trained in-house and clinically validated. These apps can be run interactively from a web browser or programmatically via a REST API with client support for multiple programming languages. Notebooks demonstrating the CGC API and pyCERR capabilities are provided at https://github.com/cerr/pycerr-notebooks. Potential applications The framework facilitates end-to-end radiological image analysis and reproducible research, including data access from public and private repositories, training and inference with AI models, and utilities for data management, visualization, and simplified access to image metadata.

title: Self-supervised multi-contrast MRI reconstruction via mask-guided frequency-domain fusion.
abstract: Background Multi-contrast magnetic resonance imaging (MC-MRI) enables detailed tissue characterization by acquiring multiple contrast-weighted images from the same anatomical region. Redundancy across contrasts can improve reconstruction from under-sampled data. However, conventional deep learning approaches rely on fully-sampled, contrast-aligned datasets, which require long acquisition times. Extended scanning durations not only increase patient burden but may also introduce physiological risks, limiting the practical adoption of accelerated MC-MRI in clinical settings. Purpose This study introduces Self-MF, a self-supervised MC-MRI reconstruction framework that leverages contrast redundancy without requiring fully sampled target-contrast labels. The framework aims to provide a high-fidelity, scalable solution for reconstructing under-sampled multi-contrast images while preserving anatomical details and contrast fidelity. Methods Self-MF implements a contrast-aware self-supervised learning strategy that randomly partitions the acquired target k-space into input and held-out subsets, allowing the model to learn joint anatomical priors from under-sampled data without fully sampled target-contrast labels. A mask-guided frequency-domain conditioning module constructs reference-conditioned auxiliary frequency channels from auxiliary contrasts and acquired target measurements, enhancing the recovery of fine structural features during score-based reconstruction. Experiments were conducted on public datasets (IXI, fastMRI) and a clinical multi-coil dataset (SIAT), spanning multiple acceleration factors and undersampling patterns to assess robustness and generalizability. Results Quantitative and qualitative evaluations demonstrate that Self-MF outperforms existing representative reconstruction methods across different contrasts, datasets, and acceleration factors. On the SIAT multi-contrast dataset, Self-MF achieved PSNR/SSIM values of 35.16/0.8870, 33.46/0.9054, and 35.31/0.9187 for T1WI, T2WI, and PDWI reconstruction under 2D random undersampling at R = 4, respectively. On the fastMRI brain dataset, Self-MF achieved 41.15 dB/0.9637 and 35.02 dB/0.8814 for T2WI reconstruction under R = 4 and R = 8, respectively, consistently outperforming the compared classical, learning-based, and diffusion-based baselines. Conclusions Self-MF provides an effective, self-supervised solution for high-fidelity MC-MRI reconstruction without fully sampled target-contrast labels. By combining contrast-aware self-supervision, frequency-domain conditioning, and diffusion-based reconstruction, the framework achieves superior image quality and robust anatomical preservation, representing a significant advancement for multi-contrast MRI in both research and clinical practice.

title: Evaluation of quantitative accuracy in 4D DCE-bCT: Insights from a perfusion phantom study.
abstract: Background Four-dimensional dynamic contrast-enhanced breast CT (4D DCE-bCT) provides submillimeter spatial resolution and temporal sampling within seconds, offering potential for improved perfusion assessment in breast cancer. Its quantitative accuracy, however, must be validated. Purpose To evaluate the accuracy of dynamic iodine concentration quantification in 4D DCE-bCT using a perfusion phantom with in-line optical spectroscopy and ultraviolet-visible (UV/VIS) spectrophotometry as reference standards. Methods A dynamic flow phantom with a 3 mm internal diameter was used to approximate tumor-feeding vessels. Potassium iodide (KI) contrast was introduced using block-pulse injections at 1, 3, and 5 mg I/mL and a gradual inflow-outflow protocol to reproduce bolus passage. In-line optical spectroscopy and UV/VIS spectrophotometry provided reference measurements. Dynamic bCT acquisitions were performed using a previously developed sparse-view protocol. A static pre-contrast scan was reconstructed with the iterative maximum-likelihood polychromatic algorithm for CT (IMPACT), and post-contrast dynamic scans were reconstructed using the prior image constrained compressed sensing (PICCS) algorithm. Acquisitions were performed at 65 kV with 0.25 mm Cu filtration, 80 mA for the pre-contrast scan (300 projections over 10 s) and 32 mA for the post-contrast scans (444 projections per 100 s), using a 5 ms pulse width. Projection data were corrected for scatter and motion before reconstruction, and the static prior was then subtracted from post-contrast volumes. Object-size effects were evaluated using the 3 mm tube and 5, 10, 15, and 20 mm hollow spheres filled with non-flowing iodine at 1, 3, and 5 mg I/mL. The tube interior was segmented using thresholding and morphological cleanup, while spherical phantoms were segmented by identifying the sphere center and extracting all enclosed voxels. Voxel values were converted to iodine concentration using a pre-determined calibration curve, and agreement with reference standards was evaluated using peak concentrations and time-concentration profiles, with errors reported as absolute and relative differences. Results In dynamic block-pulse experiments, peak iodine concentrations measured by 4D DCE-bCT were systematically underestimated relative to ground truth, with relative errors of approximately 12% to 39%. In gradual inflow-outflow experiments, the peak iodine concentration derived from 4D DCE-bCT was 5.24 ± 0.61 mg I/mL, whereas optical ground truth measured 5.17 mg I/mL. Static experiments demonstrated an average underestimation of 0.23 ± 0.14 mg I/mL across target sizes and concentrations and no relationship between iodine estimation and target size. Conclusion 4D DCE-bCT enabled acquisition of time-varying iodine concentration profiles in a 3 mm tube phantom. Gradual changes were captured more accurately compared to rapid changes, consistent with temporal averaging. These results demonstrate the feasibility of dynamic iodine imaging with 4D DCE-bCT while highlighting current limitations and motivating further evaluation in anatomically realistic phantoms and pilot clinical studies.

In gradual inflow-outflow experiments, the peak iodine concentration derived from 4D DCE-bCT was 5.24 ± 0.61 mg I/mL, whereas optical ground truth measured 5.17 mg I/mL. Static experiments demonstrated an average underestimation of 0.23 ± 0.14 mg I/mL across target sizes and concentrations and no relationship between iodine estimation and target size.

Conclusion

4D DCE-bCT enabled acquisition of time-varying iodine concentration profiles in a 3 mm tube phantom. Gradual changes were captured more accurately compared to rapid changes, consistent with temporal averaging. These results demonstrate the feasibility of dynamic iodine imaging with 4D DCE-bCT while highlighting current limitations and motivating further evaluation in anatomically realistic phantoms and pilot clinical studies.

title: A dual-prompt framework combining spatial-mask priors and clinical-text conditioning for CT-only GTV delineation in esophageal cancer: A multicenter study.
abstract: Background Accurate gross tumor volume (GTV) delineation is essential for esophageal cancer radiotherapy, but CT-only automatic delineation remains difficult because of indistinct tumor boundaries. Purpose This study aimed to develop and validate a two-stage dual-prompt framework combining a spatial-mask prior with LLaMA3-encoded clinical-text conditioning for primary esophageal GTV delineation. Methods This multicenter study included 857 patients: 500 for development, 125 for internal validation, 50 for ablation analysis, and 182 for external validation. The proposed framework consists of two stages: (1) a CT-based automatic segmentation network generating an initial GTV as a spatial mask prompt, and (2) a refinement network that jointly incorporates spatial mask prompt and LLaMA3-encoded clinical text prompt derived from structured clinical information. Performance was evaluated using overlap, surface distance, and volumetric metrics, and compared with multiple state-of-the-art deep learning models. Ablation and radiomics analyses assessed component contributions and downstream consistency. Results In internal validation, the framework achieved a DSC of 80.32 ± 6.65%, an HD95 of 11.42 ± 8.90 mm, and an absolute volume difference of 9.99 ± 10.49 mL; all Holm-adjusted p values were <0.001 versus the comparison models. Mean DSCs were 78.60 ± 13.39% and 78.36 ± 15.54% in the external cohorts. Mean DSCs were 78.60 ± 13.39% and 78.36 ± 15.54% in the two external cohorts, respectively. In external cohort A, ContextUNETR showed a lower mean HD95 than the proposed model (10.93 ± 8.03 vs. 13.44 ± 18.90 mm), although the paired difference was not statistically significant after Holm correction (adjusted p = 0.906). Compared with the direct Stage-1 output, the complete framework consistently improved overlap, boundary-distance, and volumetric-agreement metrics across the internal and both external validation cohorts (all adjusted p < 0.001). LLaMA3 encoding improved DSC versus an MLP using the same variables (adjusted p = 0.009), whereas ASSD did not differ significantly. Automatic and manual GTVs showed high radiomic concordance and comparable prognostic performance. Conclusion The framework improved overlap and volumetric agreement for CT-only primary esophageal GTV delineation across multicenter validation cohorts, although boundary-distance performance varied across external cohorts.

title: Segment anything model (SAM)-driven prompt-guided interactive delineation of gross tumor volume for rectal cancer neoadjuvant radiotherapy.
abstract: Background Segment Anything Model (SAM), a prompt-guided foundation model, exhibits substantial potential for medical image segmentation by incorporating prior knowledge through user-defined prompts. However, the application of SAM in radiotherapy target delineation remains limited. Purpose This study proposes a feasible prompt-guided interactive delineation workflow driven by an optimized SAM. Methods A total of 100 rectal cancer neoadjuvant radiotherapy cases were collected (60 for training and 40 for testing). This study utilized bounding-box prompts to guide SAM for GTV segmentation. Physicians manually draw box prompts on certain slices, while box prompts for the remaining slices are automatically generated using an interpolation strategy. Four fine-tuning strategies for SAM training were evaluated, and the impact of prompt numbers and placements was assessed as well. The performance of the finalized workflow with optimized SAM was compared with five state-of-the-art (SOTA) models, and its robustness to prompt variations in middle-slice selection and box-prompt margins was analyzed. Results Compared to other fine-tuning methods, freezing the image encoder obtained the most stable performance. Prompts on only 3 slices achieved accuracy comparable to prompts on all slices. The placement of the middle-slice prompt exhibited negligible impact (p > 0.05). The finalized SAM-driven workflow outperformed end-to-end baseline models both visually and quantitatively (3D DSC: 0.92 vs 0.80; 3D HD95: 2.73 vs 12.70; IoU: 0.86 vs 0.67; Sensitivity: 91.20% vs 85.98%; Precision: 93.65% vs 79.23%), while maintaining stable performance across certain prompt variations. Conclusions The proposed SAM-driven interactive workflow with as few as 3 box prompts achieves favorable accuracy of GTV segmentation for rectal cancer neoadjuvant radiotherapy.

title: MRpro: Open Framework for Model-Based, Learned, and Quantitative MR Imaging-Application to Low-Field MRI.
abstract: MRpro is an open-source framework for MR image reconstruction and quantitative parameter estimation, with particular relevance to low-field MRI. Built on PyTorch, it supports modern deep-learning reconstructions and standardized data exchange through ISMRMRD for raw k-space data and DICOM and NIfTI for reconstructed images and parameter maps. This facilitates integration into existing pipelines and the use of data from different devices. MRpro provides unified data structures for the consistent manipulation of MR datasets and associated metadata, together with a library of composable operators, proximable functionals, and optimization algorithms. The operator library includes a unified Fourier operator for all common trajectories and operators specifically developed for low-field applications, such as a B 0 -correction operator. Together, these components underpin ready-to-use implementations of key reconstruction algorithms. For deep learning, MRpro includes data-consistency layers, differentiable optimization layers, state-of-the-art backbone networks, and access to public datasets to facilitate reproducibility. Automated quality control supports collaborative development. We demonstrate MRpro for automatic reconstruction, iterative SENSE, deep-learning-based reconstruction, and quantitative parameter estimation. For selected Cartesian and non-Cartesian tasks, iterative SENSE reconstructions from MRpro differed from those obtained with BART, SigPy, and MRIReco by less than 3% relative RMSE. Further applications use public and simulated datasets and measured low-field data acquired at 0.3 T, 0.6 T, and 47 mT. MRpro provides a reproducible and maintainable foundation for future MR imaging research.

title: Predicting Glioma Survival From Intratumoral Vascular Topology: A Connectional Vessel Template Approach.
abstract: Gliomas exhibit aberrant angiogenesis that drives tumor progression and therapeutic resistance. Susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) enables noncontrast visualization of intratumoral vasculature, but current approaches rely on summary metrics that overlook vascular topology. We developed a graph-based framework to model vascular networks from SWI and predict glioma survival. Between 2005 and 2020, 228 adults with histologically confirmed diffuse glioma (World Health Organization [WHO] Grades 2-4) who had undergone preoperative MRI were retrospectively screened. MRI was performed on 1.5- and 3-T scanners (Siemens Healthineers, Erlangen, Germany) including T2-weighted imaging (TR/TE 4000-6000/80-120 ms, FOV 220-256 mm, slice thickness 2-3 mm) and SWI (TR/TE 25-35/15-25 ms, FOV 200-240 mm, slice thickness 1.5-2 mm). Tumors were manually delineated on T2-weighted images and coregistered to SWI using advanced normalization tools (ANTs). Intratumoral vessels were extracted from SWI using the Frangi vesselness filtering and represented as graphs with nodes at branch points and endpoints and edges along vessel segments. Node-level, edge-level, and graph-level vascular features were processed by a GraphSAGE encoder to generate patient-specific embeddings, which were compared to a learnable population template within the connectional vessel template (CVT) framework to quantify individual vascular atypicality. A Cox proportional hazards head integrated graph embeddings, template deviation, and demographic features to output risk scores. Model performance was evaluated using 10-fold stratified cross-validation for progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS), with multivariable Cox regression and subgroup analyses across isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) mutation status and histological subtypes. A total of 193 patients were included (mean age 43.4 ± 14.0 years; 57.5% male). OS analysis included 182 patients (61 deaths), and PFS analysis included 170 patients (102 progression events). The CVT model achieved C-indices of 0.812 for PFS and 0.839 for OS with significant risk stratification (PFS log-rank p = 5.82 × 10 -7 ; OS log-rank p = 1.17 × 10 -6 ). The CVT risk score independently predicted PFS (HR 1.77, p < 0.001) and OS (HR 1.44, p < 0.001) beyond age and sex. Subgroup analyses demonstrated consistent PFS discrimination in IDH-wildtype tumors and glioblastoma (C-index 0.677) and strong OS prediction in IDH-mutant tumors (C-index 0.850). Graph-based modeling of SWI-derived vascular topology provides robust, independent prognostic information for glioma survival using a single noncontrast MRI sequence.

title: Radial Tiny Golden Angle UTE (tyGA-UTE) for Cardiac MRI in the Small Animal Model.
abstract: Robust cardiorespiratory motion correction is critical for high-quality ultra-high-field (UHF) preclinical cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Whereas radial tiny golden angle (tyGA) sampling, data-driven self-gating (sg), compressed sensing (CS), and ultrashort echo time (UTE) are individually well-established techniques, their integration into a unified acquisition and reconstruction pipeline, together with systematic validation at 11.7 T remains insufficiently explored. This study presents and validates a UHF-optimized tyGA-based UTE workflow that enables high-temporal-resolution sliding-window dynamic imaging (SW-tyGA-UTE) and high-spatial-resolution cardiorespiratory self-gated cine imaging (Gated-tyGA-UTE) from a single continuous acquired tyGA acquisition. All experiments were performed on an 11.7-T small-animal MRI system in 16 healthy wild-type mice. Cardiac functional parameters, image quality metrics (signal-to-noise ratio [SNR] and contrast-to-noise ratio [CNR]), and inter-/intra-observer reproducibility were systematically compared between the proposed tyGA-UTE pipeline and two navigator-gated reference techniques: retrospectively gated FLASH and UTE methodologies. SW-tyGA-UTE and Gated-tyGA-UTE reconstructions yielded global left ventricular functional parameters comparable to those obtained with the reference methods (all p > 0.05). All functional metrics showed excellent intra-observer (ICC = 0.94-0.99) and inter-observer (ICC = 0.90-0.98) reproducibility, with ejection fraction showing the highest measurement consistency. Image quality was evaluated using an image-based within-ROI noise quantification approach that captures both thermal noise and reconstruction-related artifacts. In this analysis, the Gated-tyGA-UTE protocol showed no statistically significant differences in left ventricular blood-pool SNR, myocardial SNR, or CNR relative to the reference sequences. In contrast, the high-temporal-resolution sliding-window reconstruction showed significantly reduced image quality across all three metrics, consistent with the expected spatiotemporal trade-off of undersampled dynamic imaging. This study validates a robust, UHF-optimized tyGA-UTE imaging workflow that generates both high-fidelity quantitative cine data and ultra-fast dynamic cardiac images from a single acquisition. The unified pipeline eliminates the need for sequential repeated scans, minimizes anesthesia-related physiological variability, and improves experimental efficiency, providing a practical tool for preclinical cardiac phenotyping, longitudinal studies, and drug screening.

title: Volumetric and Intrastructural Characterization of the Substantia Nigra Using Optimized Synthetic MR Images Derived From Quantitative T1 Maps at 3 T.
abstract: Accurate imaging of the substantia nigra (SN) is critical for diagnosing and monitoring neurodegenerative conditions like Parkinson's disease. However, conventional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) struggles to precisely visualize this small structure within the deep brain due to poor intrinsic tissue contrast. Although quantitative MRI (qMRI) captures objective tissue properties with diagnostic value to assess neurodegenerative conditions of the SN, additionally acquiring multiple MRI contrasts inherently requires impractically long scan times. To overcome this, qMRI-derived synthetic MRI uses mathematical signal models to retrospectively generate various synthetic contrast weightings from a single map of quantitative T1-relaxation times (qT1). This study investigated which mathematical transformations of qT1 maps, including an approximation for pseudo-proton spin density (pPSD), are best suited to derive optimized synthetic MRI contrasts for accurate SN analysis. By evaluating six dedicated qT1-derived contrast weightings in healthy subjects, this work demonstrates that a nonlinear, signal-increased pPSD-based synthetic MRI contrast (si 4 _PSD) yields a favorable balance by significantly enhancing optical contrast while maintaining a sufficient signal-to-noise ratio and preserving contrast-to-noise ratio. The si 4 _PSD images enabled highly consistent, automated atlas-based segmentation of the SN that significantly outperformed traditional manual delineation, overcoming rater variability and bias from age-dependent contrast changes. Automated segmentation revealed significant sex- and hemisphere-dependent differences in SN volume, whereas qT1 data simultaneously uncovered distinct subregional and asymmetric intrastructural aging patterns. These findings highlight that macrostructural volume and intrastructural tissue properties must be assessed as independent variables. In conclusion, this qT1-based, automated framework offers a highly consistent, scalable approach to SN mapping without extending patient scan times. By clearly separating physiological intrastructural changes affecting MRI contrasts from mistakenly perceived general atrophy, this methodology provides a powerful foundation for developing more precise and objective imaging biomarkers for SN-related neurodegenerative diseases in both research and clinical settings.

title: Diagnostic Imaging Analysis of Humerus Bone Structure in Long-Legged Buzzard (Buteo rufinus): Radiology and CT-Scan Insights.
abstract: Advanced imaging techniques, particularly computed tomography (CT), are revolutionising veterinary diagnostics by providing detailed structural insights essential for accurate diagnosis and treatment planning. This study aimed to compare the efficacy of CT imaging and digital radiography in the diagnosis and treatment of raptors, with the goal of identifying the more precise and efficient imaging technique for clinical management. By evaluating these methods, the research seeks to optimise diagnostic accuracy and treatment planning, ultimately improving rehabilitation outcomes for birds of prey requiring high-precision care. This study evaluated the humerus bone structure of 10 adult Long-legged Buzzard (Buteo rufinus) individuals using digital radiology and CT imaging. Birds were sedated to minimise stress, and both left and right humerus structures were examined. Humerus indices, including cranio-caudal diameter, medullary cavity diameter, cortical thickness and bone density, were measured to compare the effectiveness of the two modalities. Results of this study revealed significant differences in humerus indices between radiology and CT techniques (P < 0.05), with CT providing more accurate and detailed measurements. CT excelled in visualising internal structures, such as the cortex and medullary cavity, offering superior diagnostic clarity. No significant differences were observed between left and right humerus indices (P > 0.05), indicating consistent bilateral symmetry. The study concludes that CT imaging is superior to digital radiology for assessing humerus bone structure in the long-legged buzzard, providing precise information crucial for managing humeral injuries. These findings underscore the clinical utility of CT in avian veterinary medicine, particularly for raptors and recommend This technique helps surgeons prepare the necessary equipment more accurately and use more precise methods, ultimately increasing the success rate of surgeries.

title: Gastroschisis-Like Defect in a Crossbred Bovine Calf: Anatomical, Clinical and Surgical Perspectives.
abstract: Congenital abdominal wall defects with evisceration are relatively uncommon in bovine neonates. This report describes a gastroschisis-like anomaly in a one-day-old female crossbred calf, suspected to result from the prenatal rupture of an omphalocele. The condition was characterised by evisceration of the pyloric abomasum and a portion of the small intestine through a ventral abdominal wall defect (involving the umbilical ring) without a protective sac. Clinically, the calf presented with generalised weakness, lateral recumbency and an inability to suckle. Physical examination revealed hypothermia and mild cardiorespiratory depression, while the eviscerated organs appeared viable. Hematobiochemical evaluation demonstrated hyperlactatemia, mild hemoconcentration, borderline hypoproteinemia, hypoglycemia and electrolyte imbalances, alongside elevated renal biomarkers. Radiographic examination revealed no additional abnormalities. Following stabilisation with fluid therapy and active warming, surgical management involved the reduction of eviscerated contents and closure of the abdominal defect. Intraoperative findings of membranous sac remnants supported a diagnosis of prenatal sac rupture. The calf recovered uneventfully with postoperative supportive care, achieving complete healing by Day 29. To the authors' knowledge, this is the first documented case of a gastroschisis-like defect with abomasal evisceration in a bovine calf. This condition represents a clinical emergency and should be included in the differential diagnosis for neonatal calves with ventral abdominal wall defects.

title: Left Medial Liver Lobe Torsion Associated With Hepatocellular Carcinoma in a Pembroke Welsh Corgi: A Case Report.
abstract: Liver lobe torsion (LLT) is a rare, potentially life-threatening condition in dogs and is reported most often in medium- to large-breed dogs. Neoplasia-associated LLT is unusual, and detailed descriptions of LLT associated with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) are scarce. A 12-year-old spayed female Pembroke Welsh Corgi (9.5 kg) presented with acute collapse after several months of progressive lethargy and inappetence. Laboratory abnormalities included increased alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase activities and C-reactive protein concentration. Computed tomography (CT) identified a 7.2 × 6.7 × 6.5 cm mass arising from the left medial liver lobe, a whirl sign at the base of the mass and a non-enhancing hypoattenuating region consistent with necrosis. Midline celiotomy and left medial liver lobectomy were performed without detorsion. Cytology of abdominal effusion was consistent with a culture-negative inflammatory exudate. Histopathology confirmed HCC with extensive necrosis, and the examined surgical margin was free of neoplastic cells. The dog recovered uneventfully, was discharged on postoperative Day 4 and had no recurrence of clinical abnormalities at 1-year follow-up. This case highlights the apparent association between HCC and LLT and the unusual location of the torsion axis at the base of the mass rather than at the hepatic hilus, although causality cannot be established from a single case. CT visualisation of the whirl sign at this atypical site was instrumental in establishing the preoperative diagnosis and guiding surgical planning.

title: Fingerprinting the polycystic kidney: radiomics of the noncystic parenchyma for earlier ADPKD detection.
abstract: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease risk stratification relies on total kidney volume, a validated marker of cyst burden and progression. Kremer et al.'s pilot study used rapid breath-hold magnetic resonance fingerprinting with radiomics to evaluate noncystic renal parenchyma in children and young adults. Quantitative T1/T2 texture features distinguished autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease from controls independently of total kidney volume, cyst fraction, age, or body size, suggesting early tissue changes. Small, cross-sectional, unmatched data require longitudinal validation of reproducibility, prognostic value, and clinical utility.
