title: Quantitative UTE MRI Differences in the Meniscus Following ACL Reconstruction: A Prospective Cohort Study Using 3D Ultrashort Echo Time Adiabatic T1rho and Magnetization Transfer Imaging.
abstract: Background ACLR is associated with altered joint loading and increased risk of post-traumatic osteoarthritis. Conventional MRI has limited sensitivity to early meniscal differences because of short-T2 signal decay and magic-angle effects. Purpose To evaluate whether 3D ultrashort echo time imaging-based adiabatic T1rho (UTE-Adiab-T1rho) and ultrashort echo time imaging-based macromolecular fraction (UTE-MMF) identify regional quantitative MRI differences after ACLR. Study type Prospective longitudinal cohort study. Population 30 control scans, 19 ACLR scans at 6-12 months, and 13 ACLR scans at 12+ months were analyzed. Mean ages were 34.5, 34.5, and 37.2 years; female/male counts were 15/15, 9/10, and 8/5. Field strength/sequence Participants underwent 3-T knee MRI with 3D fat-saturated UTE-Adiab-T1rho and UTE magnetization transfer sequences. Assessment UTE-Adiab-T1rho and UTE-MMF maps were generated with single-component exponential and two-pool magnetization transfer models. Values were extracted from four meniscal regions of interest by a blinded reader, with blinded redelineation in a subset. Patient-reported outcomes included International Knee Documentation Committee, Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score, and Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index scores. Statistical tests Linear mixed-effects models accounted for repeated observations. Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction was applied. Results UTE-Adiab-T1rho showed significant group (q = 0.001) and region (q < 0.001) effects. Compared with controls, UTE-Adiab-T1rho was higher in LAM at 6-12 months (+5.60 ms; q = 0.035) and 12+ months (+7.09 ms; q = 0.028), and in LPM at 12+ months (+6.35 ms; q = 0.035). UTE-MMF showed significant group (q = 0.041) and region (q < 0.001) effects. LPM UTE-MMF was lower than controls at 6-12 months (-3.56 percentage points; q = 0.028) and 12+ months (-3.10 percentage points; q = 0.049). No 6-12 versus 12+ month MRI or PROM contrast survived FDR correction. MRI-PROM associations were not FDR-significant (all q ≥ 0.383). Data conclusion UTE-Adiab-T1rho and UTE-MMF mapping identified regional MRI differences after ACLR. Pairwise differences were concentrated in lateral regions, but corrected group-by-region interactions were not significant. PROMs were worse after ACLR but did not differ between postoperative windows after correction. Evidence level 2. Technical efficacy stage 2.

Purpose

To evaluate whether 3D ultrashort echo time imaging-based adiabatic T1rho (UTE-Adiab-T1rho) and ultrashort echo time imaging-based macromolecular fraction (UTE-MMF) identify regional quantitative MRI differences after ACLR.

Study type

Prospective longitudinal cohort study.

Population

30 control scans, 19 ACLR scans at 6-12 months, and 13 ACLR scans at 12+ months were analyzed. Mean ages were 34.5, 34.5, and 37.2 years; female/male counts were 15/15, 9/10, and 8/5.

Values were extracted from four meniscal regions of interest by a blinded reader, with blinded redelineation in a subset. Patient-reported outcomes included International Knee Documentation Committee, Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score, and Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index scores.

UTE-Adiab-T1rho showed significant group (q = 0.001) and region (q < 0.001) effects. UTE-Adiab-T1rho and UTE-MMF mapping identified regional MRI differences after ACLR. Pairwise differences were concentrated in lateral regions, but corrected group-by-region interactions were not significant. title: Value of Multimodal Ultrasound Imaging With Super-Resolution in the Differential Diagnosis of Benign and Malignant Superficial Lymph Nodes: A Dual-Center Prospective Study.
abstract: Objectives Accurate differential diagnosis of benign and malignant superficial lymph nodes (LNs) is critical for clinical management. The objectives of this study were to explore the feasibility and clinical value of super-resolution ultrasound (SRUS) in the differential diagnosis of superficial lymphadenopathy and to establish and validate a multimodal ultrasound diagnostic model based on conventional ultrasound (US), contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS), and SRUS, so as to improve the accuracy of distinguishing benign from malignant superficial LNs in clinical practice. Methods A total of 200 LNs from 165 patients with superficial lymphadenectasis were prospectively enrolled from two medical centers. All patients underwent conventional US, CEUS, and SRUS imaging. Predictive models were constructed based on the conventional US, CEUS, and SRUS features in the training cohort, and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), sensitivity, and specificity were calculated to evaluate their predictive performance in the external validation cohort. Results The training cohort comprised 117 patients with a total of 140 LNs including 46 benign and 94 malignant lesions. The validation cohort included 48 patients with 60 LNs in total, with 21 benign and 39 malignant lesions. Among the models constructed based on the training cohort, the SRUS model exhibited significantly superior diagnostic performance (AUC = 0.822) to the conventional US and CEUS models (P < .05). The combined model, integrating all three modalities, achieved an AUC of 0.892 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.833-0.952) in the training cohort and 0.890 (95% CI: 0.791-0.990) in the external validation cohort, demonstrating excellent and stable diagnostic performance. Conclusion SRUS provides crucial imaging evidence for the non-invasive qualitative evaluation of LNs. The multimodal diagnostic model incorporating the features of US, CEUS, and SRUS can significantly improve the accuracy of distinguishing benign from malignant LNs.

title: Intraoperative Bone Marrow Frozen Sections Reduce Positive Final Margins in Mandibulectomy.
abstract: Objectives To assess the impact of intraoperative bone marrow frozen section (IBMFS) use on final margin status and survival outcomes in patients undergoing mandibulectomy for squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) and non-SCC neoplasms. Methods A single-center retrospective cohort study was performed of patients undergoing segmental or marginal mandibulectomy for benign or malignant neoplasms between 2009 and 2025. The medical record was reviewed for demographic data, histopathologic disease features, treatment, and outcomes. Univariable and multivariable Cox regression analyses were used to evaluate associations between IBMFS and recurrence-free and overall survival among patients with SCC. Results Of 235 cases, IBMFS were performed in 80.4%. IBMFS analysis was associated with reduced rates of positive final bone margins (1.1% vs. 8.7%, p = 0.014) and overall positive margins (7.9% vs. 19.6%, p = 0.029). Positive IBMFS rate was higher among non-SCC neoplasms than SCC (23.5% vs. 3.5%, p = 0.007), with no significant difference in rate of final positive margins. IBMFS results demonstrated 90.0% sensitivity, 99.4% specificity, and 98.9% concordance with final histopathology. Among SCC patients, IBMFS use was not significantly associated with recurrence-free survival (aHR 0.671, p = 0.320) or overall survival (aHR 0.967, p = 0.923); only nodal disease and age were significantly associated with survival. Conclusions In this retrospective single-center cohort, IBMFS use was associated with improved final margin control across tumor types, including non-SCC neoplasms. Although no survival benefit was demonstrated, its association with margin clearance suggests that IBMFS may be a useful intraoperative adjunct in mandibulectomy for head and neck neoplasms. Level of evidence: 3

title: MRI-Derived Muscle Fat Fraction Reflects Disease Severity and Functional Impairment in Charcot-Marie-Tooth Disease Type 1A.
abstract: Introduction/aims Progressive intramuscular fat infiltration is a hallmark of neuromuscular degeneration in Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A (CMT1A). Quantitative assessment of muscle fat fraction (FF) by Dixon magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides an objective biomarker of disease severity, but manual segmentation is laborious and variable. This study explored whether automated MRI-based FF quantification reflects disease severity and functional decline in CMT1A. Methods Sixty-nine genetically confirmed patients with CMT1A who underwent 3D multi-echo Dixon lower-leg MRI were retrospectively analyzed. A deep learning-based segmentation model delineated four muscle compartments (anterior, lateral, deep posterior, superficial posterior) and mean FFs were computed volumetrically. Correlations were tested between MRI-derived FFs and clinical outcomes, including the Charcot-Marie-Tooth Neuropathy Score (CMTNSv2), Functional Disability Scale (FDS), and time-, strength-, distance-, and repetition-based performance. Partial correlations were adjusted for age and body mass index. Results All compartmental and total FFs correlated positively with CMTNSv2 and FDS (r = 0.39-0.49, p < 0.05). FFs were positively associated with time-based and negatively with strength-, distance-, and repetition-based measures. FF Anterior showed moderate correlations with stair climb time (r = 0.68, p < 0.001) and 6-min walk distance (r = -0.66, p < 0.001), with similar magnitudes across compartments. Most associations remained significant after adjustment. The lateral compartment showed the highest FF (median 33.2%), consistent with the peroneal pattern of CMT1A. Discussion Automated MRI-based FF quantification provides a reproducible biomarker of disease burden in CMT1A, reflecting clinical severity and functional decline, and may serve as an imaging outcome measure in future studies.

title: Results from the VANISH study: A prospective multicenter study validating a single-nucleotide polymorphism-based noninvasive prenatal test to assess aneuploidy risk in surviving twins of vanishing twin pregnancies.
abstract: To develop and validate a single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)-based noninvasive prenatal cell-free DNA (cfDNA) screening algorithm capable of identifying the cfDNA signal of the living fetus in vanishing twin (VT) pregnancies and assessing that twin's aneuploidy risk. Prospective study enrolling participants ≥18 years old at ≥9 weeks' gestation with an ultrasound-confirmed VT at 21 US sites (August 2021 to August 2023). The study protocol specified SNP-based cfDNA screening at enrollment and at two additional 3-week intervals. Neonatal buccal swabs evaluated the SNP profile of the living fetus. Cases lost to follow-up and with missing samples were excluded. Using SNP-based technology, an algorithm to identify the living fetus was developed based on the number of fetoplacental cfDNA signals and individual fetal fraction measurements. Concordance between cfDNA in maternal plasma and newborn buccal-swab SNP profiles was used to validate the algorithm in correctly identifying the living fetus. Common aneuploidies and fetal sex were determined for the living fetus. Of 136 participants enrolled, 106 met criteria for the final analysis; 45 for development and 61 for validation. In the validation cohort, median gestational age was 10.7 weeks (range: 8.0-16.1 weeks) at ultrasound diagnosis of a VT. In 93.4% of validation cases, the algorithm identified the living fetus and gave an aneuploidy result; 90.2% within the first two blood draws. At the time the living fetus was identified, 39 samples had two fetoplacental signals and 18 had one. Aneuploidy results included 56 low-risk and one high-risk result for trisomy 21. Neonatal buccal swabs confirmed that the VT algorithm correctly identified the living twin and gave a correct aneuploidy result in 57/57 cases (100%; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 93.5%, 100.0%). Among 29 participants with all three blood draws and two fetoplacental signals at enrollment, two signals persisted in 93.1% at the second blood draw and 72.4% at the third. The SNP-based algorithm accurately identified the living fetus in VT pregnancies in this small study. Aneuploidy risk assessment was validated in all cases where the cfDNA signal for the living twin was identified, though these findings should be interpreted with caution given the limited sample size. ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05004337.

The study protocol specified SNP-based cfDNA screening at enrollment and at two additional 3-week intervals. Neonatal buccal swabs evaluated the SNP profile of the living fetus. Using SNP-based technology, an algorithm to identify the living fetus was developed based on the number of fetoplacental cfDNA signals and individual fetal fraction measurements. Concordance between cfDNA in maternal plasma and newborn buccal-swab SNP profiles was used to validate the algorithm in correctly identifying the living fetus. Common aneuploidies and fetal sex were determined for the living fetus. Of 136 participants enrolled, 106 met criteria for the final analysis; 45 for development and 61 for validation. In the validation cohort, median gestational age was 10.7 weeks (range: 8.0-16.1 weeks) at ultrasound diagnosis of a VT. In 93.4% of validation cases, the algorithm identified the living fetus and gave an aneuploidy result; 90.2% within the first two blood draws. At the time the living fetus was identified, 39 samples had two fetoplacental signals and 18 had one. Aneuploidy results included 56 low-risk and one high-risk result for trisomy 21. Neonatal buccal swabs confirmed that the VT algorithm correctly identified the living twin and gave a correct aneuploidy result in 57/57 cases (100%; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 93.5%, 100.0%). Among 29 participants with all three blood draws and two fetoplacental signals at enrollment, two signals persisted in 93.1% at the second blood draw and 72.4% at the third. The SNP-based algorithm accurately identified the living fetus in VT pregnancies in this small study. Aneuploidy risk assessment was validated in all cases where the cfDNA signal for the living twin was identified, though these findings should be interpreted with caution given the limited sample size. title: Regional growth patterns of fetal corpus callosum at 18-32 weeks' gestation assessed by three-dimensional transvaginal neurosonography.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate the normal development of the fetal corpus callosum (CC) between 18 and 32 weeks' gestation using three-dimensional (3D) transvaginal neurosonography and to assess the effect of volume contrast imaging (VCI) on the measurement of fetal CC biometry. Methods This study included two cohorts of women with a singleton pregnancy: a prospective cohort attending the research clinic at Prince of Wales Hospital in Hong Kong SAR, China, between April 2019 and February 2025, at which 3D fetal brain volumes were acquired prospectively, and a retrospective cohort attending CRIFM Prenatal Medical Clinic in Osaka, Japan, between December 2018 and March 2025, from which archived 3D fetal brain volume datasets were retrieved. In both cohorts, 3D fetal brain volume data of the CC were acquired using transvaginal neurosonography between 18 and 32 weeks' gestation using the same acquisition protocol. Inclusion criteria were appropriately grown fetuses at 18 + 0 to 32 + 6 weeks' gestation, without suspected structural or chromosomal defects. In the midsagittal plane, using 3D volume multiplanar imaging, the CC length and total area were obtained and regional thickness at the genu, body and splenium were measured following a modified Garel's method. Additionally, the areas of five vertical CC segments defined by arithmetic fractions of the CC length following Witelson's classification (anterior one-third, anterior midbody, posterior midbody, isthmus and splenium) were obtained. All fetal biometric measurements were performed using non-VCI and VCI modes. Measurements obtained using non-VCI and VCI modes were compared using the paired t-test. Generalized Additive Models for Location, Scale and Shape (GAMLSS) were used to explore the relationship between all biometric measurements of the fetal CC and gestational age. The final models were used to derive percentiles and construct reference curves. Intra- and interobserver variability were assessed using 30 randomly selected cases. Results A total of 956 fetuses at 18-32 weeks' gestation were included. Gestational age-specific trajectories of fetal CC biometry were established, demonstrating distinct, non-linear growth patterns in CC length, total area, genu, body and splenium thicknesses and the areas of five individual CC subdivisions from 18 to 32 weeks. Overall, the genu and body thicknesses increased sharply from 18 weeks to 23 weeks. Thereafter, genu thickness continued to increase gradually until 32 weeks, whereas body thickness plateaued before showing renewed growth at 31-32 weeks. The percentile curve for fetal CC total area demonstrated a steady increase from 18 to 32 weeks. Among the five subdivisions of the CC, the splenium demonstrated the most pronounced absolute area growth, reaching a median of approximately 0.40 cm 2 by 32 weeks, with markedly greater expansion than the midbody regions throughout the second to early third trimesters. Fetal CC biometric measurements were comparable between non-VCI and VCI measurements. Overall, the biometric measurements demonstrated high reproducibility, with most showing good-to-excellent intra- and interobserver reliability, except for moderate interobserver reliability for genu and body thicknesses. Conclusions We have characterized region-specific non-linear growth patterns in fetal CC development from 18 to 32 weeks, with posterior-predominant area expansion most pronounced in the splenium. The clinical significance of regional CC measurements remains uncertain, and the presented trajectories should be regarded as descriptions of normal developmental patterns rather than as reference charts for isolated clinical decision-making. Longitudinal studies incorporating postnatal neurodevelopmental assessment will be required to determine their prognostic value. © 2026 The Author(s). title: Preoperative prevalence and risk factors for thromboembolic events following tibial plateau fractures: a retrospective analysis of an underestimated risk.
abstract: Background Tibial plateau fractures (TPF) are complex intra-articular injuries carrying a high risk of deep vein thrombosis (DVT), muscular vein thrombosis (MVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE). Preoperative thrombosis is frequently clinically silent yet may cause serious complications, whereas its detection delays definitive surgery. This study assessed the prevalence and risk factors of preoperative venous thromboembolic events (VTE) in surgically treated TPF before and after implementation of routine duplex ultrasound screening. Methods In this retrospective single-centre study at a level 1 trauma centre, all adult patients surgically treated for traumatic TPF (AO 41B/C) between January 2015 and August 2025 were reviewed (547 patients, 554 fractures). Until August 2020 duplex ultrasound (DUS) was performed only on clinical suspicion; from August 2020 onward routine preoperative DUS was progressively implemented. VTE were confirmed by DUS or CT angiography. Prevalences are reported per fracture and patient characteristics per patient; regression analyses were performed at fracture level, except for the patient-related model. Results With DUS restricted to clinical suspicion (cohort A; 246 fractures), the detected prevalence of preoperative VTE was 3.7% (95% CI 1.9-6.8) and that of DVT 2.4% (1.1-5.2). Under routine screening (cohort B; 205 screened fractures) it was 20.0% (15.1-26.0) and 17.1% (12.5-22.8), respectively, 82.9% of DVT being distal. Given the different diagnostic strategies, this reflects the higher diagnostic yield of screening rather than a true increase in VTE. In cohort B, 28 of 41 VTE (68.3%) and 24 of 35 DVT (68.6%) were clinically silent. Two patients had in-hospital cardiac arrest from PE: one died from a DVT undetected before screening was introduced, the other had an asymptomatic DVT identified by screening. VTE was independently associated with pre-existing therapeutic anticoagulation (adjusted OR 2.96, 95% CI 1.10-7.98) and with the duration of external fixation (adjusted OR 1.11 per day, 1.02-1.20). High-grade closed soft-tissue injury (adjusted OR 2.41, 1.07-5.45), polytrauma (adjusted OR 2.24, 1.07-4.68) and initial external fixation (univariable OR 3.60, 1.76-7.35) were also associated with VTE, but none remained significant after accounting for fixation duration (adjusted OR 1.42, 0.52-3.89; 1.96, 0.76-5.05; 0.62, 0.12-3.27), i.e. risk was driven by time in the fixator rather than by external fixation as such. Conclusions Surgically treated TPF carry a substantial burden of preoperative VTE, and routine DUS reveals a high proportion of clinically silent thrombosis that would otherwise remain undetected. Severe closed soft-tissue injury, pre-existing therapeutic anticoagulation and, above all, the duration of external fixation may help to identify patients at increased risk. As two diagnostic rather than two treatment strategies were compared, the study cannot determine whether screening improves outcomes or reduces PE; prospective evaluation of structured screening and risk-adapted thromboprophylaxis is warranted.

title: [Hepatic postinterventional imaging : Modality selection, assessment of therapeutic response, recognition, and radiological management of typical complications].
abstract: Background Postprocedural imaging following hepatic interventions is essential for monitoring treatment success and detecting complications. Objective To provide an overview of imaging follow-up after hepatic interventions (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt [TIPS], percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography and drainage [PTCD], transarterial chemoembolization [TACE], ablation, selective internal radiotherapy [SIRT]), focusing on the selection of imaging modalities, the assessment of treatment success, and the recognition and radiological management of complications. Materials and methods Narrative review based on the current literature of hepatic radiological interventions. Results The procedure determines the choice of imaging modality. Following TIPS, functional monitoring is primarily performed using duplex ultrasound. PTCD follow-up focuses on drainage placement and bleeding complications. Following TACE and ablation, immediate hypoperfusion of the lesions is to be expected, whereas a temporary increase in size and peripheral enhancement may occur. Following SIRT, a delayed onset of the treatment effect, as detectable by imaging morphology, is characteristic. Bleeding, abscess formation, fistulas, stent occlusions or malfunctions, and tumor recurrences can be treated further using interventional radiology. Conclusion Knowledge of typical postprocedural imaging findings, as well as common complications and options for radiological treatment of complications, is crucial.

title: CT Perfusion in the differential diagnosis of glioblastomas and primary central nervous system lymphomas.
abstract: Purpose To compare perfusion parameters of glioblastomas and primary central nervous system lymphomas (PCNSL) using CT perfusion (CTP) and to assess the diagnostic performance of this technique for their preoperative differential diagnosis. Methods This single-center retrospective study included CTP data from 122 patients (57 with PCNSL and 65 with glioblastoma) examined at our hospital between 2006 and 2026. All diagnoses were histologically verified; no patient received chemotherapy, corticosteroids or radiotherapy prior to CTP. Imaging was performed on a 64-slice Optima 660 scanner (GE Medical Systems) using a prolonged perfusion protocol. title: Clinical evaluation of deep learning-based acquisition and reconstruction techniques for accelerated 2D shoulder magnetic resonance imaging acceleration at 3 T.
abstract: Purpose GE has recently developed Sonic DL MRI acceleration technology. We wished to (1) quantify scanner time reduction compared to the AIR Recon DL already in clinical use at our institution and (2) preliminarily evaluate any change in diagnostic findings between these methods. Methods A total of 30 outpatients undergoing routine shoulder MRI for shoulder pain were recruited. Each underwent routine AIR Recon DL and Sonic DL exams containing the same sequences. Three subspecialized musculoskeletal radiologists assessed image quality, graded pathology, and reported diagnostic confidence in a blinded fashion. Differences in image quality and confidence were compared using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Results Sonic DL reduced nominal acquisition time 38.7% compared to AIR Recon DL (6 min 15 s versus 10 min 12 s). Artifact was considered slightly worse on the routine examination (3.20 versus 3.37, P = 0.039); there was no significant difference in image quality, sharpness, or signal-to-noise ratio between routine and Sonic DL accelerated exams (P 0.171-0.861). Inter-reader agreement was broadly similar between routine-routine and routine-Sonic DL comparisons (median agreement 0.867 and 0.839, respectively). Within-reader analysis identified subacromial/subdeltoid bursitis and supraspinatus tendon tears more frequently on the routine protocol than on Sonic DL (P 0.049 and P 0.006, respectively). Conclusion Sonic DL enabled a 38.7% reduction in nominal shoulder MRI acquisition time with broadly comparable image quality and inter-reader agreement in this pilot cohort. Diagnostic equivalence was not established; subacromial/subdeltoid bursitis and supraspinatus tears were potentially less conspicuous on Sonic DL. A larger powered validation study would be needed to fully evaluate diagnostic performance.

title: Morphological Patterns of Fibrous-Dominant Dorsocervical Humps and a Mesh Technique for the Diffuse Subtype.
abstract: Background Fibrous-dominant dorsocervical humps remain a challenging surgical condition because dense collagen structure limits the effectiveness of conventional liposuction and adjunctive energy-based techniques. Current surgical decision-making lacks an objective framework based on the internal structural organization of fibrosis. Objective To characterize CT-based morphological patterns of fibrous-dominant dorsocervical humps and to introduce a Mesh release technique specifically designed for the diffuse fibrous subtype. Methods Preoperative axial computed tomography (CT) images from 102 patients were reviewed to evaluate the internal morphology of fibrous tissue. Two distinct patterns were identified: a localized (mass-dominant) fibrous subtype and a diffuse (septal-dominant) fibrous subtype. Diffuse cases underwent three-dimensional CT reconstruction to further characterize the spatial architecture of fibrous septa. Accordingly, a minimally invasive Mesh release technique was developed to achieve multidirectional, cross-plane disruption of the diffuse fibrous network. Clinical outcomes were evaluated using a 4-point esthetic grading scale, and complications were recorded. Results Among 102 patients, 65 (63.7%) demonstrated the diffuse fibrous subtype and underwent the Mesh release technique. CT demonstrated widespread fibrous septa without a central fibrous mass, and three-dimensional reconstruction revealed an interconnected, multi-planar fibrous network. The mean operative time was 64.6 ± 12.3 min, and the mean aspirate volume was 269.1 ± 40.9 mL. Good-to-excellent contour improvement was achieved in 90.8% of patients. Postoperative complications occurred in 23.1% of patients, including transient numbness and seroma. Conclusions Preoperative CT distinguishes localized and diffuse fibrous subtypes of fibrous-dominant dorsocervical humps. For the diffuse fibrous subtype, the Mesh release technique enables effective cross-plane disruption of the fibrous network while achieving favorable contour restoration. Level of evidence iv This journal requires that authors assign a level of evidence to each article. For a full description of these Evidence-Based Medicine ratings, please refer to the Table of Contents or the online Instructions to Authors www.springer.com/00266 .

title: Addressing unilateral lambdoid craniosynostosis using endoscopic suturectomy and barrel-stave osteotomies: surgical technique and literature review.
abstract: Purpose Unilateral lambdoid craniosynostosis (ULC) is a rare cranial deformity requiring intervention to correct asymmetry of the posterior skull. Conventional open remodeling and distraction osteogenesis offer robust expansion but carry risks of higher blood loss, hardware complications, or reoperation. We report a novel, minimally invasive technique combining endoscopic lambdoid suturectomy with barrel-stave osteotomies, supplemented by a literature review. Case description A 2-month-old healthy male presented with classic left ULC features, including occipitoparietal flattening, ipsilateral mastoid bulge, contralateral parietal bulge, and ear level asymmetry, confirmed by 3D computed tomography. Under endoscopic guidance through two small incisions, a 10-cm-long by 1.2-cm-wide lambdoid suturectomy was performed. To enhance immediate intraoperative expansion, seven 3-cm barrel-stave osteotomies were placed perpendicularly along the superior (4 cuts) and inferior (3 cuts) suture margins and gently greenstick-fractured outward. The estimated blood loss was 10 mL without perioperative complications. Postoperative cranial molding helmet therapy was initiated on day 10. At the 4-month follow-up visit, 3D surface scanning demonstrated marked improvement in head shape and symmetry. Conclusions Our method, endoscopic suturectomy and barrel-stave osteotomies on a single patient with unilateral lambdoid craniosynostosis, demonstrated safe and favorable outcomes. We believe the addition of barrel-stave osteotomies to suturectomy may yield superior clinical outcomes, compared to conventional endoscopic-assisted procedures with suturectomy alone. However, it is necessary to accumulate a larger number of cases and conduct long-term follow-up studies to further validate this hypothesis.

title: Relative frequency of non-Wilms renal tumours in children: an institutional experience from a national tertiary referral centre in Malaysia.
abstract: Purpose International protocols for paediatric renal tumours are largely based on Western data with Wilms tumour (WT) accounting for more than 90% of cases. We aimed to evaluate the relative frequency of WT and Non-Wilms Renal Tumours (NWRTs) in a diverse Asian cohort in Malaysia. Methods A retrospective review was conducted of all primary paediatric renal tumours treated at a national tertiary referral centre from 2015 to 2024. Diagnosis was confirmed via post-operative histopathology. Results Of 95 children (median age 29 months), all were Asian descent (73.7% Malay, 9.5% Chinese, 6.3% Indian). WT accounted for only 68.4% of cases, while NWRTs accounted for 31.6%. Among NWRTs, 63.3% were malignant, primarily clear cell sarcoma of the kidney (CCSK, n = 7) and renal cell carcinoma (RCC, n = 4). In the classic WT age range (6-84 months), WT prevalence was only 75.6%, with CCSK representing 9.0%. Congenital mesoblastic nephroma (CMN) predominated in infants < 6 months (71.4%), while RCC was exclusively seen in children > 84 months (40.0%). Conclusion The substantial proportion of malignant NWRTs observed in this institutional cohort highlights potential risks of neoadjuvant chemotherapy without histological confirmation. Histopathological diagnosis via percutaneous core-needle biopsy or primary surgery may be highly considered in similar clinical settings.

title: Primary and secondary vasculitis of the lung - critical evaluation of the update classification.
abstract: Vasculitis in the lung can be separated into infectious and non-infectious, and in systemic and localized ones. Three major categories in the lung are known, previously named Wegener's granulomatosis, Churg-Strauss syndrome, and microscopic polyangiitis. The classification of vasculitis was proposed in 1994, including a size distribution for each type, an antinuclear and anticytoplasmic antibody profile (ANCA), and an organ location. In an updated classification (2011) the names for two of the most common primary vasculitis were replaced: Wegener`s granulomatosis by Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) and Churg-Strauss syndrome by Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA). This proposal has been critically discussed in meetings of the pulmonary working group of ESP (2025) and the Pulmonary Pathology Society Meeting (Quebec, 2026). There were doubts about the usefulness of the when applied in pulmonary pathology. A new proposal is presented here. This classification is based on pattern recognition, such as neutrophilic, eosinophilic, and other forms of vasculitis. As many other types of pulmonary vasculitis were not covered in the old nor in the new proposal, several variants are added. This applies for example to vasculitis seen in autoimmune diseases. There is no doubt, that a classification of vasculitis is important, to sort the type of vasculitis. If possible, such a classification should be useful not only in lung pathology but more general in any other organ system. However, in several organ systems the clinical picture and the laboratory test allow a diagnosis, which is not the case in lung. On CT scan most types of pulmonary vasculitis present with ground glass opacitis with/without nodules. Often biopsies are labelled as interstitial lung disease.

title: Association of pre-closure intraoperative fibrinogen administration with early postoperative hemostasis in patients undergoing head-pelvic ring traction and three-column osteotomy for severe spinal deformity: a retrospective study.
abstract: Background Severe spinal deformity correction is associated with substantial perioperative blood loss. Evidence on pre-closure intraoperative fibrinogen administration in this setting remains limited. This study evaluated whether pre-closure intraoperative fibrinogen administration was associated with more favorable early postoperative hemostasis-related parameters. Methods This single-center retrospective study included 50 patients with severe spinal deformity who underwent head-pelvic ring traction followed by corrective surgery. Patients were classified into a fibrinogen group and a non-fibrinogen group according to whether they received pre-closure intraoperative fibrinogen administration. Postoperative coagulation parameters, hemoglobin (Hb) levels, drainage volume, and radiographic correction outcomes were compared between groups. Results Twenty-five patients were included in each group. Baseline characteristics, operative time, intraoperative blood loss, and radiographic correction outcomes were comparable between groups. Compared with the non-fibrinogen group, the fibrinogen group had lower postoperative prothrombin time and international normalized ratio, and higher prothrombin activity and fibrinogen levels (all P < 0.01). Hb levels on postoperative days 1 and 3 were higher in the fibrinogen group, whereas postoperative drainage volume and postoperative red blood cell transfusion volume were lower (P = 0.002, 0.036, 0.005, and < 0.001, respectively). No significant between-group difference was observed in Hb level on postoperative day 7. Conclusions Pre-closure intraoperative fibrinogen administration was associated with more favorable early postoperative hemostasis-related parameters in patients undergoing corrective surgery for severe spinal deformity. Given the retrospective design and potential residual confounding, these findings should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating and require validation in prospective studies.

Postoperative coagulation parameters, hemoglobin (Hb) levels, drainage volume, and radiographic correction outcomes were compared between groups.

Results

Twenty-five patients were included in each group. Baseline characteristics, operative time, intraoperative blood loss, and radiographic correction outcomes were comparable between groups. Compared with the non-fibrinogen group, the fibrinogen group had lower postoperative prothrombin time and international normalized ratio, and higher prothrombin activity and fibrinogen levels (all P < 0.01). Hb levels on postoperative days 1 and 3 were higher in the fibrinogen group, whereas postoperative drainage volume and postoperative red blood cell transfusion volume were lower (P = 0.002, 0.036, 0.005, and < 0.001, respectively). No significant between-group difference was observed in Hb level on postoperative day 7.

Conclusions

Pre-closure intraoperative fibrinogen administration was associated with more favorable early postoperative hemostasis-related parameters in patients undergoing corrective surgery for severe spinal deformity. Given the retrospective design and potential residual confounding, these findings should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating and require validation in prospective studies.

title: Computer-Aided Diagnosis of Clinically Significant Prostate Cancer in Transrectal Ultrasound.
abstract: Diagnosing clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) using transrectal ultrasound (TRUS) remains a challenging task due to limited image contrast and the subtle appearance of malignant lesions. In this study, we propose a novel hybrid framework that integrates multi-modality and multi-task learning for csPCa classification from TRUS data. The framework leverages complementary information from B-mode and strain elastography (SE) imaging via a dual-stream encoder, enhanced by cross-modal attention gate (CMAG) modules at each level. These CMAG modules first adaptively integrate cross-modal features and then employ a gating mechanism to regulate the flow of cross-modal context into each modality-specific stream. To mitigate the scarcity of segmentation annotations, we introduce a multi-scale prototype-guided learning (MSPL) strategy, which propagates supervision signals from a small set of labeled samples to unlabeled ones by leveraging learned prototypes across multiple feature scales. This design allows the task-shared encoder to benefit from structural cues captured by the segmentation branch, even with minimal voxel-level supervision. Additionally, a context-aware multi-scale classifier (CMSC) aggregates hierarchical decoder features to further exploit the synergy between classification and segmentation tasks. The proposed method is evaluated on an in-house dataset containing 612 subjects who underwent prostate biopsy and attains favorable performance in identifying csPCa with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.86. Extensive comparative and ablation results further highlight the efficacy of incorporating cross-modal interaction, prototype-guided learning, and context-aware classification for accurate and annotation-efficient csPCa diagnosis. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/mock1ngbrd/ProstateMMTNet .

title: Giant macular hole in a female patient with X-linked Alport syndrome harboring a novel de novo COL4A5 variant.
abstract: Purpose To report a female patient with genetically confirmed X-linked Alport syndrome (AS) presenting with progressive retinal thinning and giant macular hole formation. Methods A 28-year-old woman with a history of bilateral LASIK surgery was referred for evaluation of bilateral progressive maculopathy. Comprehensive ophthalmic examinations, including optical coherence tomography (OCT) and full-field and multifocal electroretinography (ERG), were performed. Targeted next-generation sequencing of COL4A3, COL4A4, and COL4A5 genes was performed. Results At presentation, decimal best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 0.7 in the right eye (OD) and 1.2 in the left eye (OS). The patient had no hearing loss or family history of renal or ocular disease. OCT revealed bilateral retinal thinning. During follow-up, progressive thinning of all retinal layers was observed, and a macular hole developed in OS, gradually enlarging from 546 µm at age 34 to a giant macular hole measuring 1684 µm in minimum diameter at age 39. At 37 years of age, full-field ERG demonstrated preserved rod system function with mild cone system dysfunction, and multifocal ERG showed significantly reduced macular responses bilaterally. Genetic testing identified a novel de novo heterozygous COL4A5 variant (p.Gly775Val), classified as pathogenic, confirming X-linked AS. Conclusions X-linked AS may present with progressive diffuse macular thinning and giant macular hole formation even in female patients without hearing loss or a family history. AS should be considered in the differential diagnosis of unexplained bilateral macular thinning and giant macular hole in women.

title: GSTP1 promoter hypermethylation in prostate cancer detection: current evidence, clinical positioning, and translational gaps.
abstract: GSTP1 promoter hypermethylation is one of the most consistently documented molecular alterations in prostate cancer, with high prevalence in malignant tissue and a well-established relationship with transcriptional silencing. However, despite more than two decades of biological and diagnostic investigation, GSTP1-based testing has not acquired a clearly defined stand-alone role in contemporary prostate cancer detection. This narrative review examines why extensive biological evidence has not translated into routine clinical use and where, if anywhere, GSTP1 testing might provide meaningful value within current diagnostic pathways. Evidence from prostate tissue, urine and circulating cell-free DNA is considered alongside the effects of biospecimen selection, preanalytical handling, CpG target selection, assay design and interpretation thresholds. Tissue demonstrates the most reproducible signal and has achieved partial clinical translation through multiplex testing such as ConfirmMDx, whereas urinary and blood-based approaches remain investigational. Recent urinary findings, including in men with moderately elevated PSA, are promising but remain preliminary and have not established incremental value beyond contemporary risk assessment, biomarkers and multiparametric MRI. The translational priority is therefore not to demonstrate again that GSTP1 detects prostate cancer, but to determine whether a standardised assay provides reproducible, nonredundant and clinically actionable information at a defined decision point. Future development should prioritise clearly specified target populations, analytically validated assay configurations, clinically significant prostate cancer as the relevant endpoint, and prospective evaluation against contemporary diagnostic pathways.

title: Artificial intelligence in gamma knife radiosurgery: applications in treatment planning, response prediction, and toxicity assessment.
abstract: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being developed across the Gamma Knife radiosurgery (GKRS) workflow, but its current applications and readiness for clinical integration remain underutilized. This narrative review examines the emerging role of AI in GKRS, with emphasis on treatment planning, outcome prediction, and post-treatment assessment. Methods A structured search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus was conducted through September 20, 2026 to identify studies applying learning-based AI approaches specifically to GKRS. Eligible studies evaluated AI models using GKRS clinical, imaging, or treatment-planning data, while non-GKRS and non-learning-based studies were excluded. Included studies were synthesized according to major stages of the GKRS workflow. Results AI applications were identified across tumor segmentation, isocenter selection and treatment planning, prescription and dose-distribution prediction, synthetic computed tomography generation, and plan-quality assessment. Post-treatment applications include longitudinal tumor monitoring and prediction of response, functional outcomes, and toxicity including peritumoral edema and radiation necrosis. Several models demonstrate promising performance, but the evidence remains predominantly retrospective and task-specific, with frequent reliance on single-center or small datasets and limited external or prospective validation. Conclusion AI has the potential to improve the consistency, efficiency, and personalization of GKRS by supporting specific technical and clinical decisions. Further multicenter validation, prospective evaluation, workflow integration, and demonstration of meaningful clinical benefit are required before routine adoption. AI currently remains a decision-support tool rather than a replacement for radiosurgical expertise.

title: Cardiovascular Toxicity Across the Cancer Immunotherapy Spectrum: Mechanisms and Management in Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor (ICI) and Chimeric Antigen Receptor T-Cell (CAR-T) Therapy.
abstract: Purpose of review This review evaluates the evolving landscape of cardiovascular toxicities associated with two pillars of modern cancer treatment: immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) and chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy. It examines their distinct immune-mediated pathophysiologies, clinical manifestations, and management frameworks. Recent findings While ICIs carry a clinical trial incidence for cardiotoxicity of approximately 1%, real-world data suggest rates of 3-5%, with myocarditis sometimes manifesting early as part of a high-mortality "Triple M" or overlap syndrome. Major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) occur in nearly 50% of ICI-myocarditis cases. Diagnosis relies on clinical presentation, biomarkers and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) using the modified Lake Louise criteria, with late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) detection sensitivity increasing from 21.6% to 72.0% when imaged after four days of symptoms. Conversely, CAR-T cardiotoxicity is predominantly driven by cytokine release syndrome (CRS), which affects 49-93% of patients with currently licensed products. Severe CRS more than doubles the risk of cardiovascular events, including a 6-10% incidence of LVEF decline and a 4-18% incidence of arrhythmias. Recent advancements include machine learning models to predict MACE and structured screening programs to risk-stratify candidates. Cardiotoxicity remains a significant complication, highlighting the need for vigilant monitoring and early intervention. Management relies on baseline risk assessment and rapid deployment of targeted therapies, such as high-dose methylprednisolone for ICI-myocarditis and IL-6 inhibition (tocilizumab) for CAR-T-related CRS. A multidisciplinary cardio-oncology approach is essential to mitigate risks. With early diagnosis and appropriate immunosuppressive strategies in a multidisciplinary setting, these complications can be better managed, optimising oncological benefits whilst reducing treatment-related morbidity and mortality in majority of patients.

title: Sonographic Evaluation of Plantar Hindfoot Pain in Athletes.
abstract: Purpose of review To provide an anatomy-based review of musculoskeletal ultrasound (US) in the evaluation of plantar hindfoot pain in athletes. This review summarizes normal sonographic anatomy, characteristic findings, diagnostic utility, and limitations for plantar fascia, heel fat pad, calcaneal, peripheral nerve, vascular, and foreign-body pathology. It also examines how US findings should be integrated with the history and physical examination in athletes. Recent findings Recent studies support high-resolution, dynamic US as a useful imaging modality for plantar hindfoot pain. US enables real-time assessment, contralateral comparison, sonopalpation, and evaluation during dynamic maneuvers. Emerging literature has further characterized the layered structure and loading behavior of the heel fat pad, dynamic sonographic findings of fat pad fracture and subluxation, and assessment of peripheral nerve entrapment. Recent studies also demonstrate that plantar fascia, heel fat pad, and other hindfoot abnormalities are prevalent in asymptomatic athletes. Although sonographic abnormalities may be associated with future time-loss injury, their low positive predictive value limits their role as a screening tool. MRI remains important when evaluating suspected calcaneal stress injury, marrow pathology, or complex soft-tissue disease. US is an accessible and valuable modality for the assessment of plantar heel pain in athletes. A structured, symptom-driven examination may improve diagnostic precision and identify alternative or coexisting pathology. Sonographic findings should be correlated with symptom location, physical examination, and sonopalpatory pain, particularly because structural abnormalities are common in asymptomatic athletes.

title: Deep learning-based renal-trauma classification: comparison of two-dimensional convolutional neural network and vision-transformer models on arterial- and venous-phase computed-tomography images.
abstract: Rapid and accurate detection of renal trauma is essential in emergency medicine. This study aimed to automatically classify renal trauma using 2D convolutional neural network (CNN) and vision transformer (ViT) models on arterial- and venous-phase computed tomography (CT) images. We analyzed CT images from 94 patients, including 47 without renal trauma and 47 with renal trauma (30,951 and 15,086 images, respectively). Arterial- and venous-phase CT images were reconstructed into axial, coronal, and sagittal images, with the renal regions cropped to construct the image datasets. Five pretrained CNN-based and five pretrained ViT-based 2D models were fine-tuned to classify renal trauma, and their performance was evaluated at the slice and patient levels using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), sensitivity, and specificity. At the slice level, the sagittal Inception-V3 model achieved the highest AUC values of 0.986 for venous-phase and 0.975 for arterial-phase images. At the patient level, the coronal Inception-V3 model achieved the highest AUC values of 0.991 for venous-phase and 0.945 for arterial-phase images. CNN-based models outperformed ViT-based models at both levels, with slice-level mean AUC values of 0.971 and 0.940 for venous-phase and 0.942 and 0.914 for arterial-phase images and patient-level values of 0.947 and 0.928 for venous-phase and 0.914 and 0.886 for arterial-phase images, respectively. The 2D models demonstrated high diagnostic performance for renal trauma, even when using arterial-phase images alone, supporting their potential for rapid decision-making in emergency settings.

title: Central Asian-Mongolian-Iranian celiac disease taskforce: A look into the future- 2026-2035 and beyond.
abstract: Background There is limited data on celiac disease (CeD) from Central Asia and Mongolia. In contrast, data from Iran shows a rapid increase in the number of diagnosed cases since early 2000s. Limited data is available and likely due to low awareness, limited diagnostic access and the current belief that CeD is uncommon. Objectives The first international Task Force for CeD met to have a look into the future at the Republican Specialized Centre of Pediatrics, Tashkent, Uzbekistan (March 2026) to (1) focus on diagnosis and prevalence research; (2) promote affordable serological testing for all socio-economic strata; (3) improve involvement of medical sub-specialties; (4) suggest proper gluten-free legislation for wheat food labeling and (5) organize affordable gluten-free food for CeD patients in general. KEY RECOMMENDATIONS (2026-2030): Standardize local tissue transglutaminase antibodies (tTGA) testing to ≤ 5-10$/test; evaluate point-of-care tests in rural clinics Conduct population-based serosurveys in Central Asia, Iran and Mongolia (n ≥ 1000 each) Advocate for mandatory gluten-free labeling standards (≤ 20 ppm) Evaluation of abdominal ultrasound in CeD recognition Establish CeD patient associations to improve patient empowerment in Central Asia, Mongolia and Iran Develop online CeD training modules for clinicians in local languages.

title: Borrelia garinii spirochetemia in a previously healthy child presenting with Streptococcus anginosus group brain abscess: a case report.
abstract: Background The clinical significance of transient Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato complex (hereafter referred to as B. burgdorferi) spirochetemia remains poorly understood and has rarely been documented. We report the isolation of viable B. garinii genospecies from the blood of a previously healthy child presenting with a Streptococcus anginosus group (SAG) brain abscess. Case presentation An eight-year-old girl presented with four days of headache, fever, nausea, slightly reduced general condition, and mild facial asymmetry. Initial evaluation, including lumbar puncture, raised suspicion of viral meningitis or Lyme neuroborreliosis (LNB). Based on the differential diagnosis of Lyme disease, she was enrolled in the prospective BRILLIANT study (NCT06045416), with additional blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) sampling for B. burgdorferi culture and serology. Following initial outpatient management, she re-presented with clinical deterioration and signs of raised intracranial pressure. Cranial magnetic resonance imaging revealed a brain abscess requiring surgical drainage. Abscess cultures yielded SAG. Dental treatment four days before symptom onset provided a plausible source of infectious spread. Treatment with intravenous ceftriaxone and metronidazole for six weeks resulted in complete clinical recovery and radiological improvement. Borrelia burgdorferi-specific two-tier serology and CSF culture remained negative. In contrast, blood plasma culture for B. burgdorferi obtained at initial presentation yielded viable spirochetes after seven weeks. Borrelia burgdorferi DNA was confirmed by flaB-targeted qPCR, and hybrid whole-genome sequencing generated a near-complete genome identifying B. garinii genospecies. Conclusion This case demonstrates viable B. garinii spirochetemia without serological evidence of LNB, incidentally detected during investigation of a SAG brain abscess. It highlights the uncertain clinical significance of transient B. burgdorferi spirochetemia, and the importance of interpreting microbiological findings within the clinical context.

title: Full-Cohort Organ Dose Assessment from Low-Dose CT Lung Cancer Screening in the National Lung Screening Trial.
abstract: Rationale and objectives Organ-specific dose estimates are needed to characterize radiation exposure from repeated low-dose computed tomography (CT) lung cancer screening in the National Lung Screening Trial (NLST). The objective was to estimate study-level doses and participant-level cumulative doses in the NLST CT screening cohort. Materials and methods This retrospective dosimetry study included 25,051 NLST CT screening participants from the Lung Screening Study and American College of Radiology Imaging Network components after excluding participants with any examination lacking a valid manufacturer-appropriate tube current-time input. Image-series metadata were linked with age, sex, height, and weight, and then valid records were grouped into 69,601 study-level screening examinations. Organ absorbed doses and effective dose were calculated using the National Cancer Institute dosimetry system for Computed Tomography with sex- and body-size-specific adult phantoms. Scan-range-related dose uncertainty was assessed with 50 stochastic simulations. Results Participants underwent a mean of 2.78 study-level screening examinations; the median study-level volume CT dose index was 3.30 mGy. Median (interquartile range) study-level lung, breast, heart wall, active marrow, and effective doses were 3.93 (3.13-4.96), 3.94 (3.14-5.04), 3.94 (3.14-5.01), and 1.26 (0.99-1.60) mGy, and 2.07 (1.65-2.59) mSv, respectively. Corresponding cumulative participant-level doses were 11.30 (8.89-14.50), 11.39 (9.01-14.75), 11.41 (8.93-14.66), and 3.63 (2.79-4.66) mGy, and 5.94 (4.69-7.64) mSv. Scan-range-related dose uncertainty was greatest for thyroid dose (mean coefficient of variation, 21.1%) and low for in-field organs. Conclusion Using NLST low-dose CT screening data, we estimated participant-level cumulative organ and effective doses and characterized variation across organs and body-size groups.

title: MRI Interpretation of Suspected Pediatric Acute Appendicitis: The Role of Pediatric Subspecialty Training.
abstract: Rationale and objectives Magnetic resonance diagnosis of pediatric acute appendicitis is highly accurate but may vary depending on reader training and subspecialty expertise. The study aims to compare the diagnostic performance of fellowship-trained pediatric radiologists and nonpediatric fellowship-trained emergency radiologists for non-contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) diagnosis of suspected pediatric acute appendicitis (AA). Materials and methods Retrospective, single-center study including 122 patients who underwent non-contrast-enhanced MRI for clinical concern of AA, following equivocal or inconclusive ultrasound. Reference standard based on clinical follow-up and surgical notes. Two fellowship-trained pediatric radiologists and two nonpediatric fellowship-trained emergency radiologists independently reviewed the examinations using a standardized yes/no case report form. Paired comparisons used McNemar's test. Predictive values are reported descriptively with 95% confidence intervals, with between-groups differences assessed using case-level bootstrap resampling. Appendix visualization was analyzed descriptively only. Results The cohort included 122 patients (63 male [51.6%], 59 female [48.4%]; median age 11 years, IQR 7-13 years, range 4-18 years), of whom 31 (25.4%) had pathology-confirmed AA. Sensitivity for MRI diagnosis of AA was similar between groups (fellowship-trained pediatric 87.1% [71.1-94.9] vs nonpediatric fellowship-trained 90.3% [75.1-96.7]; P = 1.00), with higher specificity among pediatric radiologists (97.8% [92.3-99.4] vs 84.6% [75.8-90.6]; P = 0.002). Specificity was also higher among pediatric radiologists for direct signs (98.9% [94.0-99.8] vs 86.8% [78.4-92.3]; P = 0.001) and for combined direct and indirect signs (98.9% vs 92.3%; P = 0.03), as was accuracy for MRI diagnosis of AA (95.1% [89.7-97.7] vs 86.1% [78.8-91.1]; P = 0.03) and for direct signs (94.3% vs 86.1%; P = 0.03). Positive predictive value was higher among pediatric radiologists for the diagnosis of AA, direct signs, and combined direct and indirect signs, reaching 96.2% (81.1-99.3) vs 68.4% (52.5-80.9) for direct signs (P < 0.001). originalAbstract:
Rationale and objectives

Magnetic resonance diagnosis of pediatric acute appendicitis is highly accurate but may vary depending on reader training and subspecialty expertise. The study aims to compare the diagnostic performance of fellowship-trained pediatric radiologists and nonpediatric fellowship-trained emergency radiologists for non-contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) diagnosis of suspected pediatric acute appendicitis (AA).

Materials and methods

Retrospective, single-center study including 122 patients who underwent non-contrast-enhanced MRI for clinical concern of AA, following equivocal or inconclusive ultrasound. Reference standard based on clinical follow-up and surgical notes. Two fellowship-trained pediatric radiologists and two nonpediatric fellowship-trained emergency radiologists independently reviewed the examinations using a standardized yes/no case report form. Paired comparisons used McNemar's test. Predictive values are reported descriptively with 95% confidence intervals, with between-groups differences assessed using case-level bootstrap resampling. Appendix visualization was analyzed descriptively only.

Results

The cohort included 122 patients (63 male [51.6%], 59 female [48.4%]; median age 11 years, IQR 7-13 years, range 4-18 years), of whom 31 (25.4%) had pathology-confirmed AA. Sensitivity for MRI diagnosis of AA was similar between groups (fellowship-trained pediatric 87.1% [71.1-94.9] vs nonpediatric fellowship-trained 90.3% [75.1-96.7]; P = 1.00), with higher specificity among pediatric radiologists (97.8% [92.3-99.4] vs 84.6% [75.8-90.6]; P = 0.002). Specificity was also higher among pediatric radiologists for direct signs (98.9% [94.0-99.8] vs 86.8% [78.4-92.3]; P = 0.001) and for combined direct and indirect signs (98.9% vs 92.3%; P = 0.03), as was accuracy for MRI diagnosis of AA (95.1% [89.7-97.7] vs 86.1% [78.8-91.1]; P = 0.03) and for direct signs (94.3% vs 86.1%; P = 0.03). Positive predictive value was higher among pediatric radiologists for the diagnosis of AA, direct signs, and combined direct and indirect signs, reaching 96.2% (81.1-99.3) vs 68.4% (52.5-80.9) for direct signs (P < 0.001). Negative predictive value did not differ in any category. Interpretation time was longer for pediatric radiologists, with a median paired difference of 23.5 seconds (P = 0.04).

Conclusion

Fellowship-trained pediatric radiologists had higher specificity, positive predictive value, and accuracy than non-pediatric emergency radiologists for MRI diagnosis of suspected pediatric AA, with a small difference in interpretation time (median, 24 seconds). These findings, based on a limited number of readers, suggest differences in subspecialty expertise and aims and support further multicenter evaluation.

title: Preoperative respiratory muscle strength, muscle mass, and respiratory sarcopenia as predictors of postoperative pulmonary complications after thoracic and cardiac surgery: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Background & aims Postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs) are common after thoracic, upper abdominal, and cardiac surgery and are associated with adverse outcomes. Respiratory sarcopenia (RS), characterized by coexisting reductions in respiratory muscle mass and strength, may represent a clinically relevant prognostic phenotype, but its prognostic value remains uncertain. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to assess whether low preoperative respiratory muscle mass, reduced strength, or their coexistence as RS or probable RS predicts PPCs after thoracic and cardiac surgery. Methods We searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and CENTRAL from January 1990 to February 2026 for studies relating preoperative respiratory muscle mass, strength or flow, or RS to PPCs. Risk of bias was assessed using the Quality In Prognosis Studies tool. Adjusted odds ratios (ORs) were pooled using random-effects models after harmonizing effect directions such that ORs >1 denoted higher risk. Results Sixteen studies were included; all involved thoracic or cardiac surgery, and none included an upper abdominal cohort. Cutoff-based respiratory muscle strength or flow impairment was associated with increased odds of PPCs (OR 2.25, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.50-3.37; I 2 = 51.2%), with the most consistent association observed for percent-predicted peak expiratory flow (PEF) (OR 2.03, 95% CI 1.43-2.90; I 2 = 0%). Continuous PEF was associated with PPCs, whereas ultrasound-based diaphragm indices showed smaller, non-significant associations. RS or probable RS was associated with PPCs (OR 2.08, 95% CI 1.33-3.26; I 2 = 0%). Conclusions Preoperative functional respiratory muscle impairment, particularly reduced PEF, and RS or probable RS were associated with PPCs. Given that the evidence was limited, heterogeneous, and predominantly derived from thoracic surgery, prospective confirmation is needed.

title: Comparative assessment of ultrasound and bioelectrical impedance analysis for sarcopenia screening in chronic liver disease.
abstract: Background Sarcopenia, primarily defined by low muscle mass (LMM), is associated with worse clinical outcomes in chronic liver disease (CLD). Diagnosis is challenging due to the lack of standardized tools. Ultrasound (US) offers a promising method for muscle mass assessment but requires validation against reference methods like bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA). Aim To evaluate the correlation and agreement between US- and BIA-based muscle measurements and the accuracy of US in identifying sarcopenia in patients with cirrhosis and a history of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Methods In this prospective observational study, 88 patients with cirrhosis (HCC active or under follow-up) underwent muscle mass assessment by BIA and US of quadriceps and psoas muscles. Analyses included correlations, intraclass correlation (ICC), Bland-Altman plots, and ROC analysis to determine US cut-offs for sarcopenia. Results Quadriceps US indices correlated with BIA-derived ASMM/h² (r = 0.35-0.45, p < 0.01), with high inter-rater reliability (ICC 0.83-0.96). The feather index demonstrated the best discriminative ability (AUROC 0.81, sensitivity 83%, specificity 72%) in this low-prevalence setting. Dual cut-off strategies improved screening value (negative predictive values above 97%). Conclusion Muscle US is a reliable, non-invasive screening tool for sarcopenia (specifically LMM) in CLD patients. Its use can reduce reliance on complex diagnostics, enabling early detection and improved clinical management.

title: A liquid fiducial marker for image-guided proton beam therapy of abdominal tumors.
abstract: Purpose This study compared a liquid to solid fiducial markers regarding visibility, artifact characteristics on X-ray imaging and dose perturbation for image-guided proton therapy (IGPT) of abdominal tumors. Additionally, the radio-opaque composition of the liquid fiducial marker was optimized, and the chemical stability after proton beam irradiation was analyzed. Material and methods The fiducial markers inserted into an anthropomorphic abdominal phantom were exposed to X-ray, single-energy computed tomography (SECT), dual-energy CT (DECT) and cone-beam CT (CBCT) to determine contrast-to-noise ratios (CNR) and artifacts. Proton dose perturbation estimations were performed using a Monte Carlo dose algorithm. Chemical stability following proton beam irradiation was assessed with biophysical and optical methods. Results The CNR of the liquid marker with a volume ≥ 100 μl (CNR ≤ 2.69) on 2D X-ray images was superior to the solid markers (CNR ≤ 1.72). The artifact areas (A) and severity in the CT modalities were more pronounced for the solid (e.g. , sect A ≤ 279.4 mm 3 ) than for the liquid fiducial marker (A ≤ 30.5 mm 3 ). Dose mitigation of ≥ 50% in a proton beam was calculated for solid fiducial markers, while the liquid marker less influenced the dose distribution. Increasing radio-opaque content in the liquid prototypes improved visibility (CNR ≤ 2.97) without significantly increasing artifact volume (SECT: A ≤ 40.5 mm3) or dose perturbation. No degradation of the liquid fiducial marker's chemical composition was observed. Conclusion The liquid fiducial marker demonstrated comparable visibility and chemical stability with reduced artifact generation and dose perturbation compared to solid markers, indicating superiority for IGPT of abdominal tumors. Optimization of the liquid marker composition may be considered.

title: Risk-stratified Prostate Cancer Screening in 2026: Blood- and Urine-based Biomarkers.
abstract: Prostate cancer (PCa) encompasses a broad biological spectrum ranging from indolent to aggressive disease. Although early randomized trials generated controversy regarding the benefits versus harms of screening, contemporary evidence supports screening and early detection strategies that focus on men at the highest risk of clinically significant PCa (csPCa) or International Society of Urological Pathology grade group ≥2. Current guidelines from major urological associations emphasize shared decision-making, with earlier screening considerations for high-risk populations. Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing is important in PCa screening, but its limited specificity necessitates adjunctive tools to reduce unnecessary biopsies and overdiagnosis. Risk calculators/nomograms, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), blood-based assays (including PSA derivatives and multivariable tests such as the Prostate Health Index, 4Kscore, Stockholm3, and Proclarix), and urine-based assays (including SelectMDx, MyProstateScore 2.0, ExoDx, and miR Sentinel) further refine detection. The integration of MRI and biomarkers represents modern risk-adapted screening and early detection pathways. Ongoing large-scale trials are evaluating multimodal biomarker and MRI strategies to optimize csPCa detection while minimizing harm. Overall, risk-stratified, imaging- and biomarker-driven approaches offer pragmatic and evidence-based pathways to enhance early detection of csPCa while reducing overdiagnosis and overtreatment. PATIENT SUMMARY: This short review discusses how blood and urine tests, alongside genetic risk information, can help identify the men most likely to harbor aggressive prostate cancer-enabling early detection and intervention while avoiding unnecessary biopsies and potential harm in men at low risk.

title: The triglyceride-glucose index and intramyocardial hemorrhage identify a high-risk phenotype in STEMI.
abstract: Aims The prognostic value of combining the triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index and intramyocardial hemorrhage (IMH) in STEMI is unclear. We assessed their individual and combined association with major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). Methods This retrospective study included 456 STEMI patients undergoing primary PCI. TyG index was calculated from admission blood samples; IMH was assessed by cardiac magnetic resonance. The primary outcome was MACE (median follow-up 4 years). Multivariable Cox regression, restricted cubic spline analysis, incremental prognostic assessment (C-index, NRI, IDI), and interaction testing were performed. Results MACE increased across TyG tertiles (15.79% → 27.63% → 43.42%). The highest tertile remained independently associated with MACE (adjusted HR 1.86; 95% CI 1.09-3.20). Patients with high TyG (≥8.66) plus IMH had the worst prognosis (HR 4.00; 95% CI 2.49-6.39; P < 0.001), far exceeding either factor alone. Adding the combined variable to a base model improved discrimination and reclassification (C-index 0.640 → 0.658; NRI = 0.216, P = 0.020; IDI = 0.025, P = 0.008). Neither additive nor multiplicative interaction was significant, and results were consistent in diabetic and non-diabetic patients. A significant interaction was observed between TyG index and infarct location (P for interaction = 0.037), with a stronger effect in anterior (HR 1.59) than non-anterior infarction (HR 0.75). Conclusions The TyG index independently predicts long-term MACE in STEMI. Combining high TyG with IMH identifies a high-risk phenotype with a 4.0-fold higher MACE risk and incremental prognostic value. The TyG effect is stronger in anterior infarction, suggesting infarct location should be considered in metabolic risk stratification.

title: Multisource Coronary Artery Fistula Draining Into the Coronary Sinus: Multimodality Imaging and Surgical Repair.
abstract: Coronary artery fistula (CAF) is a rare congenital coronary anomaly. Multisource CAF draining into the coronary sinus is exceptionally uncommon and anatomically complex. A woman presented with progressive exertional dyspnea and right-sided heart failure. Multimodality imaging, including transthoracic echocardiography, coronary computed tomography angiography, and invasive coronary angiography, demonstrated multisource CAFs arising from the right coronary artery and left circumflex artery draining into the coronary sinus with diffuse aneurysmal coronary dilatation. The patient underwent surgical ligation of the dominant right CAF with concomitant tricuspid annuloplasty. Postoperative imaging demonstrated successful closure of the dominant right CAF with thrombus formation within the ligated fistulous tract, whereas the smaller left circumflex artery fistula persisted, and serial follow-up demonstrated clinical improvement. Multimodality imaging is essential for diagnosis, treatment planning, and postoperative surveillance of complex CAF. Surgical repair remains an effective treatment strategy for anatomically complex fistulas associated with significant hemodynamic consequences.

title: A deep learning radiomics model based on multiparametric MRI for predicting the efficacy of neoadjuvant chemotherapy in axillary lymph nodes of breast cancer.
abstract: Objectives In this study, we developed and validated a deep learning radiomics clinical (DLRC) model integrating multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) and clinical data to predict axillary pathological complete response (apCR) in cN+ breast cancer patients receiving neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC). Materials and methods We retrospectively collected data from 221 eligible breast cancer patients. The DLRC model integrated radiomics features and deep learning scores (DL-Scores) derived from mpMRI, together with clinical risk factors, to predict apCR. Seven classifiers were employed for model construction, and the optimal classifier was selected based on classification performance to build the final model. Model performance was evaluated using the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, area under the curve (AUC), calibration curve, and decision curve analysis (DCA). Classification performance was assessed via the confusion matrix. Additionally, SHAP plots were utilized for interpretability analysis of the model. Results Multivariate analysis confirmed that progesterone receptor (PR), human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2), clinical T stage (OR = 0.258), and time-intensity curve (TIC) were significantly associated with apCR. The mpMRI based DLRC model achieved AUCs of 0.949 (95% CI, 0.912-0.986) and 0.932 (95% CI, 0.867-0.998) in the training and validation sets. SHAP analysis further revealed the interpretability of the model. The confusion matrix visually demonstrated the consistency between the predicted results and the true labels, validating the classification performance of the model. Conclusion The DLRC model effectively predicts apCR in breast cancer patients after NAC. It can serve as an auxiliary tool for clinicians in identifying potential candidates for axillary de-escalation, offering support for personalized precision treatment. We present this article in accordance with the TRIPOD-AI reporting checklist.

title: Atlas-assisted segment anything model for fetal brain MRI (FeTal-SAM).
abstract: This paper presents FeTal-SAM, a novel adaptation of the Segment Anything Model (SAM) tailored for fetal brain MRI segmentation. Traditional deep learning methods often require large annotated datasets for a fixed set of labels, making them inflexible when clinical or research needs change. By integrating atlas-based prompts and foundation-model principles, FeTal-SAM addresses two key limitations in fetal brain MRI segmentation: (1) the need to retrain models for varying label definitions, and (2) the lack of insight into whether segmentations are driven by genuine image contrast or merely inferred by learned spatial priors. We leverage multi-atlas registration to generate spatially aligned label templates that serve as dense prompts, alongside a bounding-box prompt, for SAM's segmentation decoder. This strategy enables binary segmentation on a per-structure basis, which is subsequently fused to reconstruct the full 3D segmentation volumes. Evaluations on two datasets, the dHCP dataset and an in-house dataset demonstrate FeTal-SAM's robust performance across gestational ages. Notably, it achieves Dice scores comparable to state-of-the-art baselines which were trained for each dataset and label definition for well-contrasted structures like cortical plate and cerebellum, while maintaining the flexibility to segment anatomical structures that could be templated by compatible atlas image and label sample pairs. Although slightly lower accuracy is observed for subtle, low-contrast structures (e.g., hippocampus, amygdala), our results highlight FeTal-SAM's potential as a flexible atlas-conditioned segmentation framework without requiring a separately trained model for each supported parcellation. This method thus constitutes a promising step toward clinically adaptable fetal brain MRI analysis tools.

title: Diagnostic performance and methodological heterogeneity of neuromelanin-sensitive MRI in Parkinson's disease: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) diagnosis remains primarily clinical and is often delayed until substantial neurodegeneration has occurred. Neuromelanin-sensitive MRI (NM-MRI) assesses the integrity of neuromelanin-rich nuclei affected in PD, the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc) and locus coeruleus (LC), but its diagnostic performance, technical determinants, and translational applicability remain unclear amid heterogeneity. We aimed to quantify diagnostic accuracy, determine whether performance varies across methodological approaches, and contextualise evidence from clinically relevant settings. We systematically reviewed NM-MRI diagnostic studies through December 2025. QUADAS-2 assessed risk of bias. Sensitivity and specificity were jointly pooled using a bivariate model, and AUC using random-effects meta-analysis. Subgroup analyses and exploratory meta-regressions assessed methodological heterogeneity; broader clinical evidence was synthesised qualitatively. Thirty-nine studies were included. Across 20 PD-versus-healthy-control (HC) studies (878 PD; 690 HCs), pooled sensitivity was 89.03% (95% CI 86.01-91.45%), specificity 87.02% (95% CI 82.76-90.34%), PLR 6.86, NLR 0.126, and DOR 54.37. Across 32 studies (1411 PD; 1086 HCs), pooled AUC was 0.909 (95% CI 0.884-0.929; I2 = 64.6%). No significant unadjusted differences emerged by sequence, dimensionality, segmentation, or measurement type. NM-MRI abnormalities were detectable across prodromal, early- and advanced-stage PD, although global measures showed limited discrimination between disease stages. Subregional measures captured phenotypic variation, genotype discrimination was limited, and PD-versus-ET/APS performance was promising but variable, within small, heterogeneous evidence bases. NM-MRI is a promising non-invasive imaging biomarker for PD, with strong discrimination across diverse methodological approaches. Harmonised acquisition and analysis, externally validated diagnostic thresholds, and prospective multicentre studies in clinically representative populations are needed to support future clinical implementation.
