title: Distinct spatial organization of human hippocampal perfusion and microvascular pulsatility across age
abstract: Arterial pulsation can modulate neuronal activity through mechanosensitive pathways in mice, but whether vascular pulsatility is similarly related to neural organization in humans remains unclear. Here, using 7T MRI in 35 young and older adults, we mapped cerebral perfusion and microvascular volumetric pulsatility index (mvPI) across the unfolded hippocampus and integrated these measures with histological, electrophysiological, and transcriptomic reference maps. Perfusion and mvPI exhibited distinct spatial organization and age-related differences. In young adults, perfusion preferentially corresponded to parvalbumin-interneuron density and beta/gamma distribution, whereas mvPI was associated with theta-band distribution. A number of associations detected in young adults were not detected in the older adults maps. Spectral simulations showed qualitative similarity to heartbeat-related phase resetting as one possible explanation for the mvPI-theta relationship, while spatial transcriptomics revealed perivascular enrichment of PIEZO2, a candidate mediator of vascular mechanotransduction. Together, these findings establish perfusion and tissue-level pulsatility as distinct dimensions of human hippocampal vascular organization and provide a framework for investigating their relationships with neural dynamics across aging.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Fine Needle Aspiration Cytology in Thyroid Diseases: Comparison with Histopathological Findings in Hawassa, Ethiopia
abstract: Introduction: Thyroid diseases are major health problems and among the most common endocrine disorders worldwide, including in Ethiopia. They are characterized by alterations in hormone secretion, enlargement of the thyroid gland, or both. Fine needle aspiration cytology is an important initial screening tool, and histopathologic examination is essential for the definitive diagnosis of thyroid disease. This study aimed to compare the diagnostic accuracy of fine needle aspiration cytology with histopathology in identifying thyroid diseases. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted at three health facilities in Hawassa City, Ethiopia, involving 304 patients who underwent both thyroid fine needle aspiration cytology and histopathologic examination of the same site between 30th October 2024 and 29th October 2025. FNAC results were classified using the Bethesda system, with histopathology as the gold standard. Data were entered into Kobo Toolbox, exported to SPSS version 27, and analyzed using cross-tabulation and chi-square (χ²) tests to determine diagnostic accuracy. Result: 304 patient records were included in the study. The fine needle aspiration cytology was determinate/diagnostic in 81.6% of cases. The study revealed the sensitivity and specificity of fine needle aspiration cytology to be 88.2% (CI 77.6-95.1%) and 94.4% (CI 90.6-97.1%), respectively. The false negative and false positive rates in this study were 2.4% and 4.4%, respectively. The positive predictive value was 80.3% (CI 68.7-89.3%), and the negative predictive value was 96.8% (CI 93.8-98.7%). The accuracy of fine needle aspiration cytology in differentiating benign from malignant thyroid lesions was 93.1%. Conclusion: FNAC demonstrated strong agreement with histopathology and remains a reliable, cost-effective first-line diagnostic tool for thyroid disease, particularly in resource-limited settings. Strengthening sample handling, ultrasound guidance, and adherence to Bethesda criteria may further improve diagnostic precision

title: Discrepancies in Interpretation of Japanese Radiology Report Expressions Between Radiologists and Referring Physicians
abstract: ObjectivesTo evaluate discrepancies between radiologists and referring physicians in the interpretation of diagnostic probabilities conveyed by common Japanese expressions used in radiology reports. Materials and MethodsFifteen expressions commonly used to convey diagnostic probabilities in radiology reports were selected by five attending radiologists. An anonymous online survey was distributed to 26 radiologists and 33 referring physicians at a single institution. Participants assigned a diagnostic probability (from 0% to 100% in 10% increments) to each expression. Differences in median probabilities between radiologists and referring physicians were analyzed using the Mann-Whitney U test. Variability in interpretation was assessed using interquartile range (IQR), with IQR [≥] 30% defined as substantial variability. ResultsAll radiologists (26/26) and 97% of referring physicians (32/33) completed the survey. Seven of the 15 expressions showed statistically significant differences in interpretation between radiologists and referring physicians: "c/w" (80% vs. 60%; p = 0.031), the Japanese equivalents of "present" (100% vs. 100%; p = 0.024), "suspect of" (80% vs. 70%; p = 0.007), "possibly" (50% vs. 70%; p < 0.001), "unlikely" (10% vs. 10%; p = 0.022), "cannot be ruled out" (25% vs. 40%; p < 0.001), and "not inconsistent with" (80% vs. 90%; p = 0.008). Substantial variability in interpretation (IQR [≥] 30%) was observed for four expressions: "cannot be ruled out" (IQR, 10%-40%), "s/o" (IQR, 60%-90%), "c/w" (IQR, 50%-90%), and "not inconsistent with" (IQR, 70%-100%). ConclusionThis study revealed that nearly half of the Japanese expressions commonly used to convey diagnostic probabilities were interpreted differently by radiologists and referring physicians. These discrepancies highlight the need for a standardized lexicon to improve clarity and consistency in radiology reporting. Compliance with Reporting GuidelinesThis study was conducted in accordance with the STROBE guidelines for observational studies.

title: Beyond Kidney Volume: 3D Mapping of Parenchymal, Cortical and Medullary Thickness with Disease, Anthropometry and Kidney Adiposity
abstract: Introduction: Kidney volume is associated with renal function, but conventional whole-organ measurements may miss regional changes in kidney substructures. We used magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to test whether kidney substructure volumes and three-dimensional (3D) thickness phenotypes are associated with disease, adiposity, and incident outcomes. Methods: Automated abdominal MRI segmentations from 70,270 UK Biobank participants were used to quantify left and right kidney cortex, medulla, and parenchyma volumes and mesh-based thickness maps. Mass univariate regression generated statistical parametric maps linking regional thickness to anthropometric traits and disease (CKD, type-2 diabetes [T2D], hypertension). Bidirectional causal mediation analyses were performed using kidney substructure volumetric, thickness PCs and kidney adiposity. Longitudinal changes were assessed in 2,610 participants with repeat imaging. Cox proportional hazards models tested the associations between kidney volumes and principal component (PC) scores of thickness and incident CKD, T2D, hypertension, cardiovascular disease (CVD), and mortality. Results: CKD was associated with thinning of the parenchyma and most pronounced in the medulla (87.7% left, 72.8% right), whereas associations in the cortex were mixed. In contrast, T2D and hypertension were predominantly associated with increased thickness, most extensively in the cortex (T2D: 84.39% left, 96.35% right; hypertension: 94.8% left, 99.9% right). Age-disease interactions were associated with reduced thickness across all conditions. Smaller medulla volume and lower cortical thickness mediated the association between CKD and renal sinus fat. Kidney substructure volume was inversely associated with incident CKD across all substructures and both kidney sides (p<0.05), but positively associated with incident hypertension and mortality (p<0.05). Thickness PC scores also predicted outcomes independently of volume, with PC3 in the left cortex (HR 0.91 [0.84-0.98]), reflecting inferior pole/hilar thickness, associated with incident CKD. Conclusions: MRI-derived kidney substructure volumes and 3D thickness maps provide complementary, spatially-resolved markers of kidney morphology, that are mechanistically linked to renal adiposity and future disease risk.

title: Cribriform Status at Follow-up Biopsy Is Critical for Predicting Prostate Cancer Active Surveillance Failure in the MRI Era: a Transatlantic Cohort Study
abstract: Purpose: To assess whether follow-up MRI, biopsy status, and timing of cribriform disease detection predict active surveillance (AS) failure in a contemporary transatlantic cohort. Materials and Methods. Retrospective MRI-driven AS cohort of 619 men at two academic centers (UK/USA), 2012-2024. Primary outcome: AS failure (disease-specific mortality, metastasis, grade group [GG] ≥4 progression, or post-treatment biochemical recurrence). Key exposures: final MRI and biopsy status, timing of cribriform ≥GG2 detection. Cumulative incidence was derived; independent predictors used multivariable Fine-Gray models. Results. Over median follow-up of 6.4 years, 39/619 men (6%) experienced AS failure. Cribriform ≥GG2 was detected in 82/619 (13%) on follow-up biopsy versus 24/619 (4%) at baseline, comparably in baseline GG1 (10%) and non-cribriform GG2 (9%), and only in MRI-visible tumors. Three-year AS failure after final biopsy was 31% in men with cribriform ≥GG2 versus 0-2% with stable or non-cribriform disease; 44% of failures had stable MRI. On Fine-Gray analysis, cribriform ≥GG2 was the only independent predictor of AS failure in re-biopsied men (SHR 30; 95% CI 5.2-167; P<0.001); no type of MRI progression category was independently predictive. Among 595 men cribriform-negative at baseline, 6-year AS failure after a second biopsy was 34% if cribriform ≥GG2 was detected versus 7% if still cribriform-negative. Conclusions. Cribriform status at follow-up biopsy independently predicts AS failure, whereas MRI progression does not. The three-fold higher cribriform prevalence at follow-up likely reflects baseline sampling error. Because newly detected cribriform tumours were exclusively MRI-visible, early repeat biopsy of patients with MRI-visible disease may considerably improve risk stratification.

title: Proximal sesamoid bone fatigue in Thoroughbred racehorses is associated with palmar osteochondral disease in the adjacent third metacarpal bone condyle
abstract: Abstract Background: Proximal sesamoid bone (PSB) stress fracture is a common catastrophic injury in racing Thoroughbreds that is associated with bone sclerosis and development of focal osteolysis. Standing computed tomography (sCT) enables sensitive identification of these structural changes and associations with other more common fetlock fatigue injury such as palmar/plantar osteochondral disease lesions affecting the condyles of the third metacarpal/metatarsal (MC3/MT3). Objective: To gain insight into the PSB stress fracture mechanism, we examined associations between fatigue injury prevalence in the three major metacarpophalangeal (MCP) sites: PSB, parasagittal grooves (PSG), and third metacarpal bone MC3 condyles. Study design: Retrospective clinical study. Methods: We studied 22 catastrophically injured Thoroughbred racehorses. Thoracic limbs were examined using computed tomography (CT) (n=29). Subjective CT assessment classified 58 PSBs as 32 control and 26 case PSBs with bone fatigue (transverse fracture, focal osteolysis, or severe sclerosis). Opposing joint surfaces were also studied. PSB bone mineral density (BMD) was estimated. Results: Prevalence of fatigue injury in the PSB, condyle, and PSG was 44.8% (n=26), 43.1% (n=25), and 17.2% (n=10), respectively. For MC3 condyles with POD, 88.0% had fatigue injury in the corresponding PSB (OR = 53.2). Prevalence of PSB fatigue injury was 20.0% when there was PSG fatigue injury. The odds of a PSB having fatigue injury when the opposing MC3 PSG had signs of fatigue injury was 0.25. PSBs with opposing MC3 condyles containing a POD lesion had significantly increased BMD compared with opposing control condyles. BMD was significantly increased in PSBs with structural change associated with cyclic fatigue. Conclusions: Development of PSB fatigue and adaptive PSB sclerosis is associated with POD. Stress fractures in Thoroughbreds commonly affect the MCP joint. Condylar fractures occur from PSG or POD fatigue injury. PSB fractures are also common. Our findings suggest detailed clinical assessment of PSB structural change in racing Thoroughbreds diagnosed with POD is merited as part of routine injury prevention screening.

title: Structural damage of the cervical spinal cord within and beyond the maximal compression area in mucopolysaccharidosis types I and VI
abstract: BackgroundCervical spinal cord (CSC) compression and myelopathy are frequent, severe complications in mucopolysaccharidosis (MPS) types I and VI. Early detection is critical to prevent irreversible neurological deficits and preserve quality of life. This prospective study aimed to identify quantitative neuroimaging biomarkers of structural CSC damage and myelopathy in MPS I and VI. MethodsStructural and diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the CSC was analyzed in 17 MPS I patients, 3 MPS VI patients (19{+/-}7 years), and 19 case-matched healthy controls (20{+/-}7 years). CSC macrostructure (cross-sectional area, diameters) and microstructure (fractional anisotropy [FA], radial [RD], mean, axial diffusivities) were evaluated within and beyond the maximal compression areas. ResultsMPS patients demonstrated reduced CSC cross-sectional area and anterior-posterior diameter at upper cervical levels, alongside widespread microstructural alterations (lower FA, higher RD) throughout the CSC versus controls (pFDR<0.05). Restricted foramen magnum space was associated with microstructural damage at lower cervical levels without overt macrostructural compression. Morphological and microstructural metrics were sensitive to CSC compression and myelopathy severity (pFDR<0.05). Lower CSC integrity correlated with more advanced growth retardation (p<0.001). Among patients receiving hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, earlier treatment correlated with preserved upper CSC morphology (p<0.05). Distinct neuroimaging phenotypes were observed across MPS genotypes (pFDR<0.05). ConclusionsCSC MRI provides candidate neuroimaging biomarkers for early detection and characterization of myelopathy in MPS I and VI. Structural damage extends beyond primary maximal compression areas, highlighting these markers for clinical monitoring and future therapeutic trials.

title: Privacy-Preserving Personalized Federated Learning (PPP-FL) for Medical Imaging
abstract: Federated learning (FL) is a distributed machine learning paradigm that reduces transmission costs, mitigates cross-border data sharing restrictions, and enhances privacy by keeping raw data on local devices. Clients in FL systems train local models and share only updates, which are aggregated by a central server. While this setup limits direct data exposure, FL remains vulnerable to privacy attacks. Existing attack and defense strategies have largely been developed for centralized systems, and adapting them to FL introduces new challenges due to its unique architecture and training workflow. In this work, we first propose a model inversion attack on FL systems using Deep Convolutional Generative Adversarial Networks (DCGANs) in the context of large-scale medical imaging. Our method operates under realistic assumptions about the attacker's knowledge and capabilities. We then examine the effect of client-side differential privacy (DP) in mitigating privacy leakage and incorporate personalized FL to improve model performance under DP settings. Experiments on the Brain MRI ND-5 dataset show that DCGAN-based attacks can reconstruct semantically meaningful synthetic images, revealing significant risks to the privacy of training data. Applying DP reduces attack success but introduces an accuracy trade-off, which is further overcome by personalized FL at each client side. We also evaluate how different aggregation algorithms affect both attack vulnerability and defense effectiveness, underscoring the critical role of aggregation strategies. The proposed attack-and-defense framework is model-agnostic and applicable to a wide range of FL-based systems.

title: DART: Scaling a Shape Representation Across Anatomical Classes and Imaging Modalities
abstract: Current state-of-the-art segmentation models still produce anatomically implausible shapes, such as broken vessels and fragmented glands, on the structures that are hardest to segment. Learned shape representations capture what structures look like and can help correct these errors, but most cover a fixed set of anatomical classes. Extending this coverage across classes and imaging modalities is costly because it often requires new voxel-level annotations. We propose Diffusion for Anatomical Reshaping with Text (DART), which learns a shared shape representation from segmentation probabilities. It uses anatomical descriptions to correct these probabilities without receiving medical images. Across 13 public benchmarks, absolute Dice gains reach 31% for individual gallbladder cases in CT and 10% for individual prostate cases in MRI. Using existing segmentation predictions, we scale a single shape representation from 50 to 377 anatomical classes without new voxel-level annotations for correction training. The shared representation also corrects four lesion classes absent from training and transfers from CT to MRI without retraining. Corrected labels also improve segmentation models, raising one model's Dice from 57.1% to 67.5%. The same pipeline supports annotations for 45,000 CT scans. These results suggest that sharing shape information within and across classes can reduce the need for new voxel-level annotations when extending segmentation to more anatomical classes and imaging modalities. The model is available at https://huggingface.co/Koushik45/DART-Seg

title: Beyond the Evidence Boundary: Behavioral Mirage Under Progressive Degradation in Medical VLMs
abstract: VLMs for medical image interpretation are typically evaluated on clean inputs, despite the progressive evidence loss that can occur in high stakes clinical settings. Existing robustness studies show that performance can degrade while confidence remains high, but do not establish when a previously reliable model-case pair ceases to behave reliably. We introduce a baseline-anchored framework that traces baseline-correct cases through progressive image degradation to identify an empirical evidence boundary, and define mirage as continued commitment at this boundary, regardless of correctness. Across three VLMs on three medical datasets, only MedGemma provides a sufficiently large baseline-correct pool for trajectory analysis. On VQA-RAD, the only dataset in which the question text varies, language-only answerability is associated with baseline correctness (AUROC 0.677) and with commitment at the boundary (AUROC 0.653 to 0.670). MedGemma's post-boundary behavior is heterogeneous, including direct mirage, correct recovery, mirage dissolution, consistent abstention, and oscillation, with mirage rates of 16.0 to 100.0% across dataset-modality pairs. Despite this behavioral heterogeneity, residual-stream probes decode commit-versus-abstain behavior at the boundary with AUROC of 0.895 to 0.994 under nested cross-validation. These results show that progressive evidence loss can produce persistent commitment that output entropy and abstention behavior do not consistently reflect, motivating boundary-aware evaluation, option-order controls, and improved abstention mechanisms for reliable medical foundation models operating under partial observation.

title: AdaptMIL: Domain Adaptation for Multiple Instance Learning in Digital Pathology
abstract: Pathology foundation models (PFMs) support a wide range of histopathology tasks on whole-slide images through multiple instance learning (MIL). Despite recent progress, these models remain sensitive to cross-hospital distribution shifts: performance often degrades when a task head (e.g., classification) is trained on data from one hospital and then used on data from another hospital. To address this challenge, we propose AdaptMIL, a training strategy for integrating domain adaptation into MIL training. AdaptMIL is motivated by our finding that directly applying domain adaptation objectives during MIL training can interfere with MIL aggregation learning, often resulting in performance degradation over standard training. AdaptMIL resolves this by decoupling representation-level domain alignment learning from MIL aggregation learning through a two-stage training procedure. We show that AdaptMIL improves cross-hospital performance and outperforms alternative adaptation methods across experiments spanning multiple WSI datasets, tasks, PFMs, MIL architectures, and domain adaptation objectives. AdaptMIL's code will be released upon publication.

title: LatticeRank: Spacing-Ranked Consistency for Native-Grid 3D Medical Image Segmentation
abstract: Variable voxel spacing changes more than image resolution: it alters the discrete sampling lattice, tensor geometry, and anatomical evidence available to a 3D segmentation network. While conventional pipelines restore images to a canonical grid, direct-grid deployment requires the model itself to tolerate these changes. We observe that candidate grids are not exchangeable views -- a coarse grid removes more structural information than a mildly resampled one -- yet standard consistency objectives assign them equal influence. We therefore propose LatticeRank, a training-only framework that aligns candidate posteriors in physical space and allocates consistency supervision by voxel-spacing order: among endpoint-matched candidates, the auxiliary loss concentrates on the coarsest requested grid, while inference retains a single network forward with no candidate branch or ensemble. On MSD Task04, LatticeRank improves coarse-grid Extra Dice over mean consistency by 0.03436 across five seeds while meeting the prespecified reference-grid noninferiority criterion. A controlled ladder shows that grid exposure provides the largest recovery, posterior consistency adds a second gain, and spacing-ranked allocation yields the strongest direct-grid result; requested spacing thus provides a simple, model-independent ordering signal for direct-grid consistency learning.

title: Reliability-Guided Vision-Language Decoding with Text-Aware Skip Refinement for Medical Image Segmentation
abstract: Medical image segmentation remains challenging when targets exhibit limited visual distinction, irregular structure, or substantial variation across imaging modalities. Medical text can reduce this ambiguity, but indiscriminate fusion may introduce unreliable guidance. We present RELiF, a vision--language framework that integrates text through reliability-guided decoding. Its Reliability-guided Fusion Gate (RFG) adaptively controls cross-modal updates, while the Text-guided Skip Refinement Adapter (TSRA) refines high-resolution features using text guidance. RELiF is evaluated on radiographic, CT, and endoscopic segmentation tasks, where it shows competitive performance across diverse imaging characteristics and target appearances. Additional analyses examine efficiency and stability. The complementary uncertainty representation derived from the reliability response also shows an association with prediction difficulty, with higher uncertainty values occurring more frequently in pixels associated with segmentation errors. Code: https://github.com/SeivanTalaie/RELiF.

title: CAPS: Clinically-Verifiable Anatomy-Prioritized Synthesis for Missing MRI Imputation in Brain Tumor Segmentation
abstract: Multi-parametric MRI is the gold standard for neuro-oncology, yet acquiring complete 4-modality protocols may be unfeasible in real-world clinical practice. When handling missing modalities, existing automated systems force a critical compromise: robust segmenters operate as uninterpretable "black boxes" that bypass image generation, while standard synthesis models often produce blurry reconstructions lacking diagnostic reliability. To address this issue, we propose CAPS, a Clinically-Verifiable Anatomy-Prioritized Synthesis framework that reconciles computational precision with clinical transparency. Our multi-modal generative architecture is driven by a hybrid objective function (L_1 + L_AFP + L_DualDice) that explicitly enforces the preservation of deep anatomical features and strict topological boundaries, rather than relying solely on pixel-wise optimization. Evaluated comprehensively on the BraTS Adult Glioma dataset, the framework achieves superior synthesis fidelity across intensity-based metrics, and demonstrates robust downstream segmentation performance (82.38% mean Dice), successfully restoring verifiable visual context. Furthermore, the framework exhibits exceptional zero-shot cross-domain generalization, maintaining high structural fidelity across completely unseen Meningioma, Pediatric, and Sub-Saharan African cohorts without domain-specific adaptation. Finally, a blinded radiological assessment confirms that our anatomy-aware approach significantly enhances both perceived image quality and clinical utility, providing clinicians with the reliable visual evidence required to trust downstream automated workflows.

title: Convergent Performance, Divergent Mechanisms in LoRA-Adapted Vision Foundation Models for Brain MRI
abstract: Adapting Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) to medical imaging via LoRA has become standard practice, yet model selection is guided almost entirely by downstream task metrics, treating backbones with similar performance as interchangeable. We investigate whether equal performance implies equal internal representational shift. We analyse four ViT-B/16 backbones, DINOv3, SigLIP2, MerMED-FM, and BiomedCLIP, pre-trained with different objectives (self-distillation vs. contrastive vision-language) and on different data domains (natural vs. medical images). We adapt each to brain tumour segmentation and evaluate on six datasets covering both segmentation and Alzheimer's disease classification. Using attention divergence, weight-change analysis, and activation patching, we find that the four models converge to similar segmentation performance (mean Dice 78-81%) through markedly different internal dynamics, yet diverge in cross-task transfer: segmentation adaptation improves Alzheimer's disease classification for DINOv3 but degrades it for the other three backbones. We reveal a dissociation between modification magnitude and causal importance: the most heavily modified layers are not the causally relevant ones, with early-to-mid layers identified as sufficient for segmentation recovery. Restricting LoRA to these layers matches or approaches full-layer segmentation while reducing classification degradation in the three affected backbones, providing a mechanistically grounded strategy that is more parameter-efficient and more robust than standard full-layer adaptation.

title: CPVB-RG: Cross-Prior Visual Bridging for Prior-Aware Chest X-Ray Report Generation
abstract: Radiologists interpret follow-up chest X-rays by comparing current and prior examinations to identify new, resolved or progressing findings. Most report generation systems either omit this longitudinal context or fuse prior features without distinguishing interval changes from anatomy that remains stable over time. We propose CPVB-RG, a prior-aware framework that combines current and prior radiographs with available clinical text. Its Cross-Prior Visual Bridge (CPVB) contains Progression-Guided Focus Attention (PGFA) and two Cross-Attention units. PGFA is designed to contrast progression-difference attention with shared-spatial attention, aiming to reduce invariant responses whilst retaining coarse spatial correspondence between examinations. The Cross-Attention units then connect the resulting longitudinal visual evidence with clinical semantics. CPVB-RG is trained in two stages, using prior-guided image-text alignment followed by autoregressive report generation with a lightweight language decoder. Experiments on MIMIC-CXR and IU X-Ray show consistent improvements across language and clinical metrics. On MIMIC-CXR, CPVB-RG achieves 0.2847 F1RadGraph and 0.6692 VLScore, with statistically significant gains over the closest decoder-matched prior-aware baseline. These results support the effectiveness of the proposed difference-aware and spatially guided fusion design for prior-aware chest X-ray report generation.

title: AGGR-Mamba: Mamba-based Network with Attention-Guided Gated Residual Refinement for Undersampled MRI Reconstruction
abstract: Undersampled magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reconstruction aims to recover high-quality images from partially acquired k-space data, thereby reducing scan time. However, missing frequency-domain measurements often lead to residual aliasing artifacts, blurred edges, and loss of local structural details. In this paper, we propose AGGR-Mamba, a lightweight output-stage residual refinement method built upon a Mamba backbone for undersampled brain MRI reconstruction. The Mamba backbone first produces an initial reconstruction, and the proposed refinement modules then correct the remaining local errors and high-frequency artifacts in a controlled residual manner. Specifically, an Attention Refine Head is introduced to recalibrate local anatomical structures, edge textures, and residual-error regions through channel and spatial attention. In addition, a GDFN-style gated residual refinement branch is designed to selectively preserve informative residual features while suppressing redundant or unstable responses. By combining attention-based recalibration with gated residual selection, AGGR-Mamba improves local structure recovery without substantially disturbing the backbone reconstruction. Experiments are conducted on the IXI brain MRI dataset with T1- and T2-weighted images under acceleration factors of R=4 and R=8. The results show that AGGR-Mamba achieves competitive PSNR and SSIM performance across different reconstruction settings, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed output-stage refinement strategy.

title: A Multi-Agent Framework for Automated Machine Learning with Evidence-based Planning for Medical Image Analysis
abstract: Deep learning has become the default tool for medical image analysis, driven by the open-source movement. However, achieving the best performance on a given task remains difficult, with architecture selection and hyperparameter optimization (HPO) still considered "more of an art than a science". Automated machine learning (AutoML) automates parts of model training, yet helps little in medical imaging: general-purpose approaches lack medical architectures and preprocessing, and medical-focused ones demand engineering expertise and remain confined to narrow tasks such as 3D segmentation. We introduce MedicalMLOmni, a multi-agent AutoML framework that automates model training for diverse single- and multi-modal medical tasks through a natural language interface. Specifically, MedicalMLOmni performs evidence-based planning by retrieving published results to guide model selection and configuration, and employs parallel HPO where multiple agents explore adjustment strategies concurrently. MedicalMLOmni achieves the best score on 19 of 20 benchmarks; PMC-VQA is the exception, where a vision-language model with broader pre-training leads. Backbone-matched controls attribute the gains to the framework, not the backbone. By removing coding requirements, MedicalMLOmni lowers the barrier for domain experts with rich datasets but limited engineering expertise.

title: Brain2Vec: A Self-Supervised 3D Foundation Model for Structural Brain MRI
abstract: Deep learning models have become essential tools in medical imaging, yet training them end-to-end for diverse tasks remains challenging due to limited labeled data and computational constraints. To address this, we introduce Brain2Vec, a foundation model pre-trained on 74,425 T1-weighted Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scans pooled from multiple studies. Brain2Vec can serve both as a weight initialization backbone for fine-tuning downstream tasks and as a standalone feature extractor. We evaluated Brain2Vec in three tasks: downstream predictive performance, convergence speed, and embedding quality. Using Brain2Vec's pretrained weights as initialization and fine-tuning on labeled data for a brain age prediction task, results demonstrate improved final accuracy and faster convergence compared to random initialization. Additionally, its frozen embeddings outperform anatomically defined volumetric features on four of five downstream classification tasks and perform competitively with a state-of-the-art foundation model pre-trained on substantially more data. Lastly, we show that Brain2Vec encodes information primarily from a spatially localized and neuroanatomically meaningful set of brain regions, and that manipulating a subset of latent features produces monotonic, region-specific effects on the reconstructed anatomy. Brain2Vec code and trained models are available as an open-source package on https://github.com/CBICA/Brain2Vec. Users can apply Brain2Vec locally by installing the package, or directly through the NiChart cloud platform https://cloud.neuroimagingchart.com, where Brain2Vec features can be derived without requiring local installation or specialized infrastructure.

title: Improved three component IVIM fitting using physics-informed neural network with multimodal spatial prior
abstract: Purpose: To mitigate parameter degeneracy and improve robustness of IVIM fitting, a multimodal physics-informed neural network was developed to leverage anatomical information through the combined use of cross attention, selective spatial gating, and anatomy-weighted spatial prior. Methods: T1w and FLAIR anatomical images were co-registered to IVIM signal in native space and segmented by tissue type. The proposed Physics-Anchored Cross-attention Embedding network (PACE) encoded IVIM signals and their anatomical features in parallel branches, then integrated them via cross attention and spatial gating. An anatomy-weighted spatial prior further constrained signal reconstruction using anatomically similar neighboring voxels. PACE and its prior-guided variant were compared with two baseline deep neural networks (DNN and IVIM3C), least squares, non-negative least squares, and maximum a posteriori fitting models. All models were evaluated on signal and parameter reconstruction accuracy and lesion contrast fidelity using data generated from subjects drawn from the University of Rochester COVID cohort. Results: PACE variants demonstrated lower RMSE for all IVIM parameters except for Dmv. The anatomy-weighted spatial prior further reduced RMSE across all five parameters relative to the default PACE, with modest reductions in lesion contrast accuracy for fmv and fint. For in-vivo evaluation, PACE with spatial prior also showed the best signal reconstruction across all noise levels while maintaining good to excellent ICC. Conclusion: Multimodal anatomical information improved IVIM fitting accuracy and robustness, with selective spatial integration via cross attention, gating, and anatomy-weighted spatial prior. Keywords: intravoxel incoherent motion, physics-informed deep learning, diffusion MRI, multimodality fusion, attention mechanism

title: MedBOE: Optimization-Based Estimation of Complete Patient Body Models from Whole-Body Medical Imaging
abstract: True whole-body medical imaging captures a patient from head to toe and provides comprehensive anatomical and/or functional information. This coverage enables reconstruction of the external body surface, yielding patient body models. However, scanner geometry (e.g., bore diameter), patient characteristics, and positioning can leave body regions missing (e.g., lateral arms/torso, hands, forearms, elbows), producing incomplete patient body models. Such incompleteness limits downstream medical analyses, including derivation of body-habitus metrics (BHMs), such as body volume and surface area, for injected radiotracer activity regimens, cardiometabolic risk assessment, and computational anatomical modeling for medical imaging simulation and radiation dosimetry. We present the Medical Body model Optimization-based Estimator (MedBOE), an automated, training-free framework for estimating complete patient body models from whole-body images with missing body regions. Our innovation is to leverage the Skinned Multi-Person Linear (SMPL) template, a parametric body mesh representing a broad range of body shapes and poses, in medical imaging. MedBOE aligns the SMPL template to the incomplete patient body models via attribute-guided optimization and estimates missing body regions through geometrically and volumetrically constrained deformation. We evaluated MedBOE using two public datasets: AutoPET (91 whole-body PET-CT images) and Human Implicit Tissues (HIT; 40 whole-body segmentations from MRI images). MedBOE achieved the best overall volumetric and geometric performance among evaluated methods. BHMs derived from MedBOE were within 2% error, suggesting low percentage errors for downstream analyses. MedBOE offers an automated, training-free method for estimating complete patient body models from whole-body images with missing body regions.

MedBOE achieved the best overall volumetric and geometric performance among evaluated methods. BHMs derived from MedBOE were within 2% error, suggesting low percentage errors for downstream analyses. MedBOE offers an automated, training-free method for estimating complete patient body models from whole-body images with missing body regions.

title: Artificial Intelligence Predicts Failure of Nonoperative Treatment in Degenerative Posterosuperior Rotator Cuff Tears.
abstract: Purpose To develop an artificial intelligence-based algorithm to predict success of nonoperative treatment in degenerative posterosuperior tears and to identify the most influential features. Methods Patients with degenerative rotator cuff tears initially treated nonoperatively were enrolled prospectively from January 2022 to November 2024. Exclusion criteria included age >75 years; <24 months of follow-up; massive, traumatic, and partial tears; arthritic changes (Hamada >2); and severe fatty degeneration (Goutallier >2). All patients followed a standardized physiotherapy protocol and could choose surgery if symptoms persisted; failure was defined as opting for surgery. Collected variables included demographics, comorbidities (diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension, hypothyroidism, and smoking), magnetic resonance imaging tear characteristics (size; International Society of Arthroscopy, Knee Surgery, and Orthopaedic Sports Medicine classification; associated cuff involvement; and biceps pathology), corticosteroid injection history, and functional scores (American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons score, Subjective Shoulder Value, and the visual analog scale). First, a standard statistical analysis between groups was performed. Later, the dataset was split into a train (80%) and test (20%), and a random forest algorithm model was developed. Finally, SHapley Additive exPlanations values were computed to assess feature importance. Results Of the 412 patients enrolled, 347 patients met the inclusion criteria. After 24 months, 66 (19%) patients opted for surgery. Mean follow-up was 30.4 months (range, 24-32). Compared with the successful nonoperative treatment group, patients who failed treatment were younger (58.5 vs 64.6 years, P = .001) and had higher body mass index (28.8 vs 27.2, P = .016), greater subscapularis involvement (13.5% vs 3%, P = .042), higher visual analog scale scores (7.7 vs 7.2, P = .018), lower Subjective Shoulder Value (30.9 vs 38.9, P = .003), and lower American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons scores (40.6 vs 47.1, P = .001). The model achieved an area under the curve of 84%, predicting success rate of the nonoperative treatment with 94% sensitivity, 62% specificity, 89% positive predictive value, and 77% negative predictive value. The most influential variables for the model were age, tear size, and pretreatment functional scores. Conclusions The artificial intelligence-based algorithm accurately predicted nonoperative treatment outcomes in degenerative posterosuperior rotator cuff tears (area under the curve 0.84, sensitivity 94%). Age, tear size, and function were the main predictors. Level of evidence Level IV, prognostic retrospective case series.

title: Tumour Antigen-Specific Antibody Signatures as Diagnostic Biomarkers for Melanoma.
abstract: Early detection of melanoma remains challenging, and minimally invasive diagnostic tools are needed to complement imaging and histopathology. Circulating tumour antigen-specific antibodies (Abs) are promising biomarkers, but their diagnostic value across melanoma stages is not fully established. Circulating IgG and IgM Abs were profiled in plasma from two independent melanoma cohorts, early-stage (n = 65) and advanced-stage (n = 77), alongside healthy controls (n = 86) and individuals with prior cancer in remission (n = 37). A protein microarray containing 263 tumour antigens, predominantly cancer-testis (CT) antigens, was used to measure plasma antibody (Ab) reactivity. Univariate and multivariate ROC analyses identified candidate diagnostic biomarker signatures. Early-stage melanoma was best distinguished by an IgM signature comprising AURKA, BAGE3, BAGE4, CDK7, CEP290, MYBL2, PIAS2, RAD51 and SPANXB1 (AUC = 0.939). An IgG signature including ANKRD45, BCL2L14, CDK2, MAGEA4v3, MAPK3 and RBM46 achieved AUC = 0.827. Advanced-stage melanoma exhibited broader Ab repertoires, including an IgG signature (CTAG1A, DKKL1, PIWIL2, SPANXN1, TSGA10, TSPY1; AUC = 0.865) and an IgM signature (CPXCR1, CSAG2, FMR1NB, FOXR2, LIPI, MAGEA5, TSGA10; AUC = 0.889). Individuals in cancer remission displayed persistent Ab signatures distinct from early melanoma and healthy controls. Overlap between IgG and IgM repertoires was minimal, highlighting complementary discriminatory value. Circulating IgG and IgM Abs against tumour antigens reveal stage-specific signatures that distinguish melanoma from healthy individuals and those in cancer remission, identifying candidate discovery-stage diagnostic biomarker signatures warranting independent validation in larger prospective cohorts to determine clinical utility.

title: Contrast-Enhanced Ultrasound in the Diagnosis of Parotid Gland Castleman Disease in a Child.
abstract: Castleman disease is a rare lymphoproliferative disorder that infrequently involves the parotid gland. We report a 16-year-old girl with a 3-year history of slowly progressive, painless right cheek swelling. CT and MRI showed an avidly enhancing, markedly T2-hyperintense parotid lesion, suggesting a vascular malformation; fine-needle aspiration yielded reactive lymphoid tissue. Contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) demonstrated rapid, intense, homogeneous enhancement, confirming a hypervascular solid mass rather than a vascular malformation and raising suspicion for Castleman disease. Superficial parotidectomy confirmed unicentric hyaline-vascular Castleman disease. CEUS aided differentiation of a hypervascular solid lesion from a vascular malformation and narrowed the differential.

title: Sonographic Diagnosis and Anatomic Mapping of a Radial Artery Pseudoaneurysm Following Transradial Cardiac Catheterization.
abstract: Radial artery pseudoaneurysm is a rare complication of transradial catheterization. We report a 74-year-old woman on rivaroxaban who developed a pulsatile distal forearm mass 1 day after transradial cardiac catheterization. High-frequency ultrasound showed a rounded extra-arterial lesion (7.6 × 8.9 × 7.0 mm) not involving all wall layers, with thrombus, a discrete communicating neck, turbulent bidirectional "yin-yang" color Doppler, and preserved distal flow. Anatomic mapping showed the lesion abutting adjacent tendons and the palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve. Surgical excision and microscopic repair succeeded. Sonographic characterization provided anatomic detail that, with clinical and surgical assessment, informed individualized management.

title: Age- and sex-specific values of regional bone mineral density from opportunistic CT of the lower lumbar spine, pelvis, sacrum, and proximal femur.
abstract: Objective Standard osteoporosis assessment using dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) provides limited 2D measures (BMD, T-score), potentially missing localized bone density differences relevant to fracture risk. Opportunistic CT allows comprehensive 3D volumetric bone density analysis. This study presents a detailed 3D statistical model of CT-derived apparent volumetric bone mineral density (CT-vBMD) covering the L4 and L5 vertebrae, pelvic bones, sacrum, and proximal femur and examines spatial distributions and associations with age and sex. Materials and methods Retrospective analysis included 330 routine abdominal CT scans (ages 20-91; approximately balanced by sex). Bones were segmented with a semi-automated workflow, internally calibrated, registered to bone-specific population templates, and projected onto corresponding tetrahedral meshes. Whole-bone averages were compared across age groups and between sexes. For each element, we calculated mean vBMD, variability, correlations with age and sex, and cluster-defined low-density and age-sensitive subregions. Results The global spatial pattern was similar in females and males. The highest CT-vBMD values were localized mainly to cortical load-bearing zones, whereas the lowest values were concentrated in trabecular spongiosa. Older age was associated with lower whole-bone CT-vBMD in all bones and with stronger negative associations in trabecular-rich regions, such as the subchondral acetabulum, femoral neck, sacral ala, and vertebral bodies. Cortical-dominant load-bearing regions showed weaker negative associations with age. Conclusion This framework maps anatomically localized associations between age and CT-vBMD beyond the regions routinely assessed by DXA. Opportunistic CT mapping may complement standard osteoporosis assessment by providing spatial information for the pelvis, sacrum, lower lumbar spine, and proximal femur.

title: Machine learning-based CT radiomics for identifying high risk esophageal varices of bleeding in hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract: Purpose Esophageal variceal (EV) bleeding is a lethal complication in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Current risk stratification relies on invasive endoscopy or systemic surrogates of liver cirrhosis. This study aimed to develop a machine learning model utilizing EV-specific CT radiomics to identify high-risk esophageal varices, as defined by endoscopic criteria, in patients with HCC. Methods 151 HCC patients were enrolled and divided into a training cohort (n = 101; 75 high-risk; January 2017 - December 2022) and an independent temporal validation cohort (n = 50; 29 high-risk; January 2023 - December 2024). Endoscopic stigmata were used as an endpoint, including active bleeding or varices with high-risk features. Radiomic features were extracted from contrast-enhanced CT images acquired within six months prior to endoscopy. Model performance was evaluated using the area under the curve (AUC) of receiver operating characteristic (ROC), Brier score, calibration curves, and decision curve analysis (DCA). Results In the training cohort, the varix-specific radiomics signature developed via the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) demonstrated excellent discriminative power (cross-validated AUC: 0.956; 95% CI 0.872-1.000). In the temporal validation cohort, this model maintained high generalizability, yielding an AUC of 0.926 (95% CI 0.846-0.984, sensitivity: 93.1%, specificity: 71.4%) as well as a Brier score of 0.1186 and good calibration (intercept = -0.157, slope = 1.354). Surface-to-Volume Ratio (SVR) and NGTDM Coarseness are feasible radiomics. Conclusion The varix-specific radiomics model provides highly sensitive and mathematically stable non-invasive risk stratification for EV bleeding in patients with HCC.

title: A Next-Generation Approach to Subglandular Breast Augmentation Using B-Lite Implants: The Feather Touch Technique.
abstract: Background Awake subglandular breast augmentation offers rapid recovery but requires effective perioperative analgesia. This study evaluated a standardized multilayer fascial plane anesthetic protocol for Feather Touch technique. Methods In this prospective study, 66 women underwent primary subglandular breast augmentation between January and November 2025 under light intravenous sedation with ultrasound-guided interpectoral, pectoserratus, serratus anterior, and subcutaneous infiltration. Results All procedures were completed without conversion to general anesthesia. Early recovery was uneventful in most patients. Four minor postoperative events were recorded: double-bubble deformity, bottoming out, palpable margins, and superior malposition. No major complications occurred. Lightweight implants were associated with improved early positional stability. Conclusions A standardized multilayer fascial plane protocol can be safely integrated into awake subglandular breast augmentation using the Feather Touch technique. Matching anesthetic delivery to subglandular dissection supports intraoperative comfort and early recovery, while implant weight may influence early stability. Level of evidence iv Breast Surgery. This journal requires that authors assign a level of evidence to each submission to which Evidence-Based Medicine rankings are applicable. This excludes Review Articles, Book Reviews, and manuscripts that concern Basic Science, Animal Studies, Cadaver Studies, and Experimental Studies. For a full description of these Evidence-Based Medicine ratings, please refer to the Table of Contents or the online Instructions to Authors www.springer.com/00266.

title: Bilateral Ultrasound-Guided Erector Spinae Plane Block versus Serratus Anterior Plane Block for Postoperative Analgesia in Breast Reduction Surgery: A Prospective, Randomized, Outcome Assessor- Blinded, Controlled Trial.
abstract: Background Breast reduction surgery is a common aesthetic procedure associated with significant postoperative pain. Effective analgesia plays an important role in reducing opioid consumption, minimizing adverse effects, facilitating postoperative recovery, and improving patient satisfaction. Fascial plane blocks have recently gained popularity for breast surgery. This randomized study aimed to compare the effects of bilateral erector spinae plane block (ESPB) and serratus anterior plane block (SAPB) on postoperative analgesia in patients undergoing breast reduction surgery. Methods Seventy female patients undergoing bilateral breast reduction surgery were randomly allocated into two groups: ESPB (Group ESPB, n = 35) and SAPB (Group SAPB, n = 35). Blocks were performed bilaterally under ultrasound guidance, with 20 mL of 0.25% bupivacaine each side, 30 min before surgery. All procedures were performed using the wise-pattern reduction mammoplasty technique with a superiomedial pedicle by the same surgical team. Postoperative analgesia included intravenous paracetamol, ibuprofen, and intravenous tramadol patient-controlled analgesia (PCA). Primer outcome was 24-h tramadol consumption through intravenous patient-controlled analgesia (PCA). Secondary outcomes included time to first analgesic requirement from PCA, postoperative pain scores (NRS), intraoperative remifentanil consumption, perioperative variables, length of hospital stay, and adverse effects. Results Primary-outcome data were available for 35 SAPB and 34 ESPB patients. Mean 24-hour tramadol consumption was 70.0 ± 37.7 mg with SAPB and 53.2 ± 29.1 mg with ESPB (mean difference, SAPB minus ESPB, 16.8 mg; 95% confidence interval, 0.5-33.0 mg; p = 0.043). Median time to first analgesic requirement was 420 min with SAPB and 630 min with ESPB (log-rank p < 0.001). Pain scores did not differ significantly. Nausea occurred in five SAPB patients and no ESPB patients (Fisher's exact p = 0.054); vomiting occurred in either group. Bradycardia occurred in one ESPB group patient (p = 1). Conclusions In this single-center trial, ESPB was associated with lower 24-h tramadol consumption and a longer time to first PCA demand than SAPB, while pain scores were comparable. Level of evidence ii This journal requires that authors assign a level of evidence to each article. For a full description of these Evidence-Based Medicine ratings, please refer to the Table of Contents or the online Instructions to Authors www.springer.com/00266 .

title: Effectiveness of prenatal predictors for congenital diaphragmatic hernia on survival to discharge and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation requirement: a retrospective cohort study.
abstract: Introduction Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) is associated with high mortality and morbidity. Antenatal counselling enables parents to prepare for the postnatal outcomes and relies on effective prognostic tools. Ultrasound (USS) predictors including observed/expected lung head ratio (o/e LHR) and liver position, are used independently, or combined into severity classifications. The aim was to evaluate the association between USS predictors, and severity classifications with survival to discharge and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) requirement in prenatally diagnosed CDH at Birmingham Women's and Children's Hospital (BWC). Methods CDH patients from BWC with dates of birth between 1st December 2013-1st December 2023 were retrospectively collected. Study inclusion required o/e LHR measurement between 22- and 32-weeks gestational age (GA.) Comparisons between groups was assessed by Fisher exact test and Mann-Whitney U test. Logistic regression was performed to determine prognostic ability, with area under curve (AUC) calculated. Results 91 eligible patients were identified, which included 82 left-sided, and 9 right-sided CDH. Overall, 55% survived to discharge and 13% required ECMO. In the left CDH cohort, 57% of infants survived to discharge, and 15% required ECMO. O/e LHR, liver position and the combined predictive model including o/e LHR and liver position were predictive of survival to discharge with good prognostic ability (AUC 0.769, AUC 0.703, and AUC 0.823, respectively). O/e LHR, liver position, and the combined predictive model were not predictive of ECMO requirement. In the right CDH patients, 33% survived to discharge, O/e LHR and liver position were not predictive of survival to discharge. Conclusion O/e LHR, liver position and the combination of these predictors, predicted survival to discharge in prenatally diagnosed left CDH with the combined model, the most predictive particularly in the isolated left CDH sub-group. Further analysis into effective predictors for ECMO requirement, and for right and complex left CDH is required.

title: Diagnostic accuracy of standard practice wrist MRI for scapholunate ligament injuries: a retrospective arthroscopic correlation study.
abstract: Introduction The scapholunate ligament is the most injured intercarpal ligament. Untreated tears can lead to carpal instability and subsequent radiocarpal and midcarpal osteoarthritis. While wrist arthroscopy remains the gold standard, the diagnostic performance of standard practice preoperative MRI in clinical practice warrants further investigation. Methods We retrospectively analysed patients who underwent preoperative wrist MRI followed by wrist arthroscopy between 2013 and 2021. MRI findings regarding scapholunate ligament integrity were compared with arthroscopic findings serving as reference standard. Sensitivity and specificity were calculated for detection of any scapholunate ligament lesion (partial or complete tear). Results A total of 889 patients were included. Complete paired data were available for 864 patients with a mean age of 42.4 ± 15.4 years (range 10-83 years). 51.3% were male. MRI classified the ligament as intact in 83.9%, partially ruptured in 9.1%, and completely ruptured in 6.9%. Arthroscopy identified intact ligaments in 78.2%, partial tears in 12.9%, and complete tears in 8.9%. In this cohort, MRI demonstrated high specificity (91.1%, 95% CI 89.0-93.3) but limited sensitivity (42.0%, 95% CI 35.0-49.1) for scapholunate ligament lesions. Conclusion In standard clinical practice, preoperative wrist MRI shows high specificity but insufficient sensitivity for detecting scapholunate ligament injuries. In this cohort, MRI detected intact ligaments reliably, but a relevant proportion of partial and complete tears remained unrecognized.

title: Modic changes, chronic low back pain, and lifestyle and mental health factors: a cross-sectional analysis of a cohort study.
abstract: Purpose Modic changes (MC) are vertebral endplate and adjacent bone marrow MRI findings that have been associated with chronic low back pain (CLBP), although their clinical relevance remains debated. This study examined whether MC presence and extent are associated with CLBP status, pain intensity, and disability, and whether lifestyle or mental health factors moderate the MC-pain relationship. Methods This exploratory cross-sectional sub-study included 239 adults: 135 with CLBP and 104 controls without. Lumbar MRI scans were evaluated for MC presence, type, craniocaudal extent of vertebral body involvement, and transverse extent of endplate involvement. Firth penalized logistic regression examined associations of MC presence, type and extent with CLBP status. Linear regression models examined associations between aggregated MC count and vertebral body and endplate extent with low back pain intensity and disability within CLBP and control groups. Moderation analyses tested whether sleep disturbance, physical activity, anxiety, depression, or pain catastrophizing modified the association between MC count and low back pain intensity among individuals with CLBP. All models were adjusted for age, sex, smoking, and body mass index. Results Any MC were associated with higher odds of CLBP (OR 2.50, 95% CI 1.45-4.30; p = 0.001), with similar associations for Type 1 and Type 2 MC. Greater vertebral body involvement showed a graded association with CLBP, with > 50% vertebral body involvement associated with the highest odds (OR 4.88, 95% CI 1.14-20.92; p = 0.033). Among individuals with CLBP, aggregated MC count (β = 0.30, 95% CI 0.05-0.55; p = 0.019) and vertebral body extent (β = 0.11, 95% CI 0.01-0.21; p = 0.039) were associated with higher pain intensity, but not disability. Endplate extent was not associated with pain or disability. None of the examined lifestyle or psychological factors significantly moderated the MC-pain association. Conclusion This exploratory analysis revealed that MC, particularly those with greater vertebral body involvement, were associated with CLBP status and low back pain intensity. Lifestyle and psychological factors were related to pain severity but did not significantly modify the MC-pain relationship. These findings suggest that MC extent may be a clinically relevant imaging characteristic, although longitudinal studies are needed to clarify causality and prognostic significance.

title: Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow: from diagnosis to rehabilitation.
abstract: Background Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow (UNE) is the second most common entrapment neuropathy of the upper limb, involving physical medicine and rehabilitation, neurology, orthopedics, and plastic surgery. It results from static or dynamic ulnar nerve instability, cubital tunnel syndrome, or space-occupying lesions. Accurate diagnosis requires thorough history, clinical examination, and selection of appropriate diagnostic tests. Search strategy PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus and Web of Science were searched (January 2000-August 2026) using combinations of "ulnar neuropathy", "cubital tunnel syndrome", "elbow", "ultrasound", "electrodiagnosis", "conservative treatment", "rehabilitation" and "surgery". English-language original studies, systematic reviews and meta-analyses were eligible; case reports were included only where no higher-level evidence existed. Approximately 220 records were screened; 58 were retained, following SANRA recommendations for narrative reviews. Discussion High-resolution ultrasound provides dynamic, non-invasive, cost-effective evaluation of the ulnar nerve and real-time assessment of compression or instability, and guides minimally invasive procedures such as perineural injections, although the only randomized placebo-controlled trial did not show superiority of corticosteroid injection over placebo. Conservative treatment is usually first-line, although surgery may be required in advanced or refractory cases; comparative evidence shows no clear superiority among surgical techniques, while endoscopic decompression carries a higher complication rate than open approaches. Conclusions This narrative review summarizes current evidence on diagnostic pathways and therapeutic options for UNE, highlighting the role of ultrasound as both a diagnostic and interventional tool, and outlines gaps in the literature regarding standardized conservative and surgical protocols.

title: 3D-DDN Faster R-CNN: Pulmonary Nodule Detection Through Cross-Slice Feature Fusion and Dynamic Displacement Modeling.
abstract: Accurate pulmonary nodule detection in computed tomography (CT) remains challenging because small- and low-contrast nodules may resemble vessels and other anatomical structures on individual axial slices. We propose 3D-DDN Faster R-CNN, a multi-slice detection framework that incorporates structured local axial context into a two-stage detector. The five-slice interactive blending (5-SIB) strategy organizes five consecutive CT slices as an ordered contextual group and preserves slice-specific feature streams extracted by a shared two-dimensional backbone. The cross-slice feature fusion (CSFF) module applies slice-wise spatial self-attention at shallow feature levels and learnable cross-slice aggregation at deep feature and region-of-interest levels. The dynamic displacement constraint (DDC) models proposal displacement across adjacent slices using a positive-sample regression loss and a margin-based negative-sample contrastive loss, while a class-weighted focal loss alleviates foreground-background imbalance. The model was evaluated on a private hospital dataset, LIDC-IDRI, and LNDb using patient-level data partitions. On the private hospital dataset, 3D-DDN achieved an average precision at an IoU threshold of 0.5 (AP 0.5 ) of 75.80% ± 1.05%, a sensitivity of 89.33% ± 1.91%, and a competition performance metric (CPM) of 91.20% ± 1.50%. The corresponding AP 0.5 values on LIDC-IDRI and LNDb were 66.27% ± 0.45% and 48.20% ± 0.30%, respectively. Ablation experiments showed that direct five-slice stacking degraded performance, whereas structured feature fusion and displacement supervision recovered the performance loss and improved the overall detection profile. These results indicate that ordered cross-slice representation, hierarchical feature fusion, and proposal-displacement supervision provide complementary mechanisms for incorporating local three-dimensional context.

title: M4DTrack: A DICOM-Based Imaging Informatics Workflow for User-Supervised 4DCT Lung Tumor Motion Reporting.
abstract: Four-dimensional computed tomography (4DCT) is routinely used in radiotherapy simulation to evaluate respiration-induced tumor motion, but the motion information is often reviewed visually rather than captured as structured, phase-resolved data. We developed and evaluated M4DTrack, a DICOM-based imaging-informatics workflow for user-supervised 4DCT lung tumor motion analysis and structured, exportable three-dimensional center-of-mass (CoM) motion reporting. M4DTrack imports phase-resolved DICOM CT images, groups images by respiratory phase, displays linked axial/coronal/sagittal views, supports crosshair-based tumor localization and HU inspection, and applies seed or linked 3D-box initialization with sequential phase-to-phase HU-volume propagation. An 8-case lower-lobe lung 4DCT dataset (80 respiratory phases) was analyzed. Directional amplitudes, 3D vector amplitude, maximum phase-wise displacement, and agreement with independent ITV-GTV reference amplitudes were quantified. HU-weighted CoM amplitudes were 2.44 ± 1.44 mm, 2.64 ± 1.37 mm, and 6.04 ± 2.48 mm in X, Y, and Z patient-coordinate directions, respectively. Mean 3D vector amplitude was 7.26 ± 2.50 mm, and mean maximum phase-wise 3D displacement was 6.20 ± 2.10 mm. Biases versus ITV-GTV reference amplitudes were 0.01, - 0.84, and 0.23 mm for X, Y, and Z, respectively, with a 3D vector amplitude bias of - 0.29 mm. M4DTrack provides a user-supervised imaging-informatics bridge between qualitative 4DCT cine review and structured quantitative motion documentation. The pilot results support feasibility for generating exportable, phase-resolved tumor-motion metrics while preserving user-supervised review of 4DCT artifacts, HU-capture uncertainty, adjacent anatomy, and differences between CoM-based and extent-based measurements.

title: Artificial intelligence decision support for breast ultrasound: potential to reduce benign biopsies.
abstract: Purpose The purpose of this study is to evaluate the potential impact of a Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-cleared artificial intelligence (AI)-based decision support tool for breast ultrasound in reducing benign biopsies. Methods This study was conducted at two academic medical centers from March to May 2025 following the clinical implementation of an FDA-cleared AI-based decision support tool for breast ultrasound interpretation (Koios DS; New York, NY). Fourteen breast imaging radiologists documented BI-RADS 4 (suspicious) cases, along with the corresponding AI output. AI assessments were compared with biopsy pathology results to characterize AI classification within this selected cohort. Results Overall, 271 lesions in 253 women (mean age, 54 years; range, 24-92 years) were categorized as BI-RADS 4 and were biopsied, aspirated, and/or surgically excised. Of these, 23.2% (63/271) yielded malignant pathology, while 76.8% (208/271) were benign. The AI tool classified 90.5% (57/63) of malignant lesions as BI-RADS 4 and 9.5% (6/63) as BI-RADS 2 or 3. Among benign cases, the AI tool assigned 41.8% (87/208) as BI-RADS 2 (benign), 18.8% (39/208) as BI-RADS 3 (probably benign), and 39.4% (82/208) as BI-RADS 4 (suspicious). Retrospective application of the AI output to biopsy triage decisions suggests the potential for reduction in benign biopsy recommendations, with 60.6% (126/208) of benign lesions classified by the AI tool as BI-RADS 2 or 3. Conclusion AI may help reduce benign biopsy recommendations among lesions assessed as BI-RADS 4 by radiologists; however, careful integration with radiologist judgment and clinical history is essential to ensure timely cancer diagnosis.

title: A breast clinical scoring system to identify women with Idiopathic granulomatous Mastitis.
abstract: Purpose Idiopathic granulomatous mastitis (IGM) is a benign inflammatory breast condition that can resemble mastitis or malignancy clinically and radiographically. We aimed to develop a quantitative scoring system, based off the Komen Inflammatory Breast Cancer (IBC) scoring system [1], evaluating clinical and radiologic features to distinguish IGM from benign and malignant breast conditions. Methods We conducted a retrospective chart review of biopsy-proven IGM patients diagnosed from 2014 to 2025 via institutional electronic medical records. Clinical symptom onset, features, and diagnostic imaging were analyzed. A continuous scoring scale (1-50) was created, encompassing three categories: symptom onset, clinical features, and radiographic findings. Scores of IGM patients were compared with those of patients diagnosed with IBC, mastitis (lactational and non-lactational), and locally advanced breast cancer (LABC). Welch's two-sample t-test assessed statistical differences, and Youden index identified the optimal score threshold for predicting IGM. Results Among 148 IGM patients, predominantly Hispanic (56.8%) and Asian (26.7%), the mean age was 37.2 years, older than mastitis patients and younger than IBC patients. Key clinical features included pain or painful breast mass (100%), fistula or draining wound (77.7%), erythema (94.6%), and phlegmon (87.8%). Imaging revealed mass with collection in 84.6% and multiple masses/collections in 38.9%. The mean IGM score (35.5) was significantly higher than scores for IBC, mastitis, and LABC groups (14.4, 18, and 15.2, respectively; p ≤ 0.05). A score ≥ 24.5 predicted IGM with 93% sensitivity and 95% specificity. Conclusions This novel scoring system provides an objective framework to differentiate IGM from similar breast conditions, facilitating early diagnosis and guiding appropriate management. Clinical trial number not applicable.

title: Incidence of intra-axial brain metastases in Eastern Finland.
abstract: Purpose Brain metastases (BM) incidence and characteristics remain poorly defined due to registry data being often incomplete, recording only primary tumors or unspecified metastases. The objective of this study was to examine BM incidence rates and characteristics confirmed by MRI in North Savo, Finland. Methods In this retrospective study, North Savo residents with first MRI diagnosis of BM between 1 January 2004 and 31 December 2023 were identified through the radiology information system, irrespective of primary cancer diagnosis date. Medical and histopathological records were reviewed. Population person-years were estimated by summing annual end-year counts of all North Savo residents obtained from Statistics Finland. Crude incidence rates and age-standardized incidence rates (ASIRs), standardized to the 2013 European Standard population, were calculated. Temporal trends were assessed using age-adjusted Poisson regression. Results Among 516 patients, 474 had histopathological verification. Cancers originating from lung and breast tissue accounted for 56.8% of BM cases. Overall crude incidence was 10.22 (95% CI 9.36-11.15) and ASIR was 9.20 (95% CI 8.42-10.04) per 100,000 person years. ASIR increased from 5.8 in 2004-2008 to 11.8 in 2019-2023. Age-adjusted Poisson regression estimated a 24% increase in incidence per five-year period (incidence rate ratio 1.24; 95% CI 1.14-1.34; P < 0.001). Age-specific incidence peaked at 33.1 per 100,000 person years among patients aged 70-74 years. Conclusions MRI-confirmed BM incidence increased over 20 years, despite age standardization. Incidence was highest among older adults. These findings provide contemporary population-based epidemiological data of BM incidence.

title: Non-contrast CT radiomics for identifying nonfunctioning kidneys: a multicenter development and external validation study.
abstract: Purpose In urological practice, the decision to resect or preserve a kidney with obstruction, tumor or atrophy is based on split renal function, although SPECT renal dynamic scintigraphy as the reference standard is resource-intensive. We developed and externally validated a non-contrast CT radiomics model to identify nonfunctioning kidneys and support urological decision-making in this setting. Methods In this three-center retrospective study (TRIPOD+AI), adults underwent non-contrast CT and SPECT renal dynamic scintigraphy within 72 h. IBSI-compliant radiomics features were extracted with PyRadiomics, and between-kidney asymmetry features were constructed. After three-stage selection (Spearman, recursive feature elimination, and LASSO), 12 machine learning models were developed and externally validated in 2 independent cohorts. A Rad-score and clinical nomogram were also derived. Results Among 1029 patients, the internal cohort included 418 patients. Twenty-three of features were retained. The random forest model yielded an internal test AUC of 0.9426, sensitivity of 85.5%, specificity of 88.3%, and negative predictive value of 95.6%. Its external AUCs were 0.875 and 0.913. The nomogram attained external AUCs of 0.920 and 0.881. At the thresholds fixed in the training data, the random forest achieved external sensitivity of 66.0 and 76.4% with negative predictive values of 94.8 and 93.3%, and the nomogram 92.5 and 93.7% with 98.3 and 97.2%. Both radiomics models outperformed logistic-regression baselines built from clinical variables and simple CT size and asymmetry measurements, although the margin over the combined baseline was not statistically significant in one external cohort. The Rad-score was correlated with single-kidney GFR (ρ = -0.738, P < 0.001) and facilitated risk stratification. Conclusion Non-contrast CT radiomics identified nonfunctioning kidneys without contrast agents or radiotracers. Because non-contrast CT is already part of routine urological workup, this externally validated rule-out tool may reduce unnecessary SPECT examinations and support decisions between nephrectomy and nephron-sparing management.

In this three-center retrospective study (TRIPOD+AI), adults underwent non-contrast CT and SPECT renal dynamic scintigraphy within 72 h. IBSI-compliant radiomics features were extracted with PyRadiomics, and between-kidney asymmetry features were constructed. After three-stage selection (Spearman, recursive feature elimination, and LASSO), 12 machine learning models were developed and externally validated in 2 independent cohorts. A Rad-score and clinical nomogram were also derived.

Results

Among 1029 patients, the internal cohort included 418 patients. Twenty-three of features were retained. The random forest model yielded an internal test AUC of 0.9426, sensitivity of 85.5%, specificity of 88.3%, and negative predictive value of 95.6%. Its external AUCs were 0.875 and 0.913. The nomogram attained external AUCs of 0.920 and 0.881. At the thresholds fixed in the training data, the random forest achieved external sensitivity of 66.0 and 76.4% with negative predictive values of 94.8 and 93.3%, and the nomogram 92.5 and 93.7% with 98.3 and 97.2%. Both radiomics models outperformed logistic-regression baselines built from clinical variables and simple CT size and asymmetry measurements, although the margin over the combined baseline was not statistically significant in one external cohort. The Rad-score was correlated with single-kidney GFR (ρ = -0.738, P < 0.001) and facilitated risk stratification.

Conclusion

Non-contrast CT radiomics identified nonfunctioning kidneys without contrast agents or radiotracers. Because non-contrast CT is already part of routine urological workup, this externally validated rule-out tool may reduce unnecessary SPECT examinations and support decisions between nephrectomy and nephron-sparing management.

title: Evidence for Embedding Smoking and Vaping Cessation Support in Primary Care: A Scoping Review.
abstract: Background Smoking is a leading preventable cause of disease, with vaping creating new public health concerns. This review synthesised evidence on interventions and strategies to integrate cessation care into primary healthcare. Methods We conducted a systematic scoping review of PubMed and EMBASE for studies published between 19 September 2020 and 19 September 2024. Eligible studies evaluated smoking and/or vaping cessation interventions or implementation strategies in primary care settings in high-income countries (Australia, Canada, EU, UK, USA). Two reviewers independently extracted data on study characteristics, intervention types, outcomes, and abstinence verification. Results Of 2166 records screened, 30 empirical studies were included. Most focused on smoking cessation, with only two addressing e-cigarette users. The strongest evidence supported multi-component interventions combining behavioural counselling and pharmacological treatments. Implementation strategies included electronic health record prompts, cost-free pharmacotherapy, financial incentives, and integration of cessation support into low-dose computed tomography screening or post-spirometry feedback. Evidence for the effectiveness of provider education was inconclusive. Conclusions The evidence supports several interventions and implementation strategies for integrating smoking cessation into primary care, though data on vaping cessation are limited. These findings will inform the development of targeted approaches to enhance cessation support in primary healthcare.

title: Primary cardiac angiosarcoma: From pathogenesis to therapeutic strategies.
abstract: Primary cardiac angiosarcoma (PCAS) is a rare yet highly aggressive malignancy arising from cardiac vascular endothelial cells. This tumor predominantly affects young to middle-aged males and carries a dismal prognosis, typically characterized by a median survival of less than one year. Owing to its nonspecific manifestations and rapid infiltrative growth, most patients present at an advanced or metastatic stage. Recent genomic and transcriptomic studies have revealed molecular drivers in PCAS, including recurrent mutations in POT1, KDR/VEGFR2, and PLCG1, loss of CDKN2A, and aberrant angiogenic cascade activation. In parallel, an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment dominated by exhausted T cells and tumor-associated macrophages may collectively contribute to tumor progression and therapeutic resistance. Multimodal imaging, integrating echocardiography, cardiac magnetic resonance, computed tomography, and PET/CT, plays a central role in detection, tissue characterization, and systemic staging. Histopathology with immunohistochemistry remains the diagnostic gold standard. Current treatment strategies rely on multimodal approaches, including surgery, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy, with emerging targeted therapies and immunotherapies under active investigation. Despite recent advances, clinical outcomes remain poor, highlighting the urgent need for improved mechanistic understanding and more effective personalized therapeutic strategies.
